items.descriptionOriginal: My grandad was, simply put, the man. He fought in World War II , lived into his 90s with the strength and vigor of a much younger man, and made an unforgettable impression on everyone who knew him. He was truly a force of nature that I was lucky to have in my life. He was also a highly quotable man, full of incredible one-liners . When I was a kid and my family would visit and he was ready to wrap things up, he’d cheekily say “Well, we certainly have seen you,” and, “Come again when you can’t stay so long.” My Greatest Generation grandad also loved to entertain. Though not a man of many words, he was a legendary host. His advice to us grandkids about being a great conversationalist was always the same: Can you believe there was a time that being polite and of high-character was more important than being charismatic? Photo credit: Britt Ful/Flickr “Always ask the last question.” That was it. That was his key to never running out of things to say in a conversation. It sounds extremely obvious, but you’d be surprised how contrary it runs to a lot of the advice young people are getting now. In certain sectors, the name of the game is all about how to be more charming and more charismatic. “Self-help” forgets that the real key to being interesting is being interested in what the other party has to say. What made my grandad’s execution of this simple concept great was his confidence in the fact that they didn’t have to be great questions. He would just keep asking them, like a steamroller. He knew that, if he kept it up, he’d eventually hit on something that would launch a deeper and more interesting discussion. Conversations were often logistical at first: How was the drive? What time did you leave? Was there any traffic? Where’d you stop to eat? What did you order? Before you knew it, you were off and running. That was the beauty of the technique. Asking questions, of course, is not new advice! It’s been around forever, and it’s still preached heavily today by psychologists and master small-talkers. Research backs it up: Harvard Business School’s Alison Wood Brooks and her colleagues found that people who ask more questions, especially follow-up questions , tend to be better liked by their conversation partners, which is exactly what Grandad’s “last question” is all about. Why so many people don’t ask But anybody who’s been in conversation with another human being lately knows that a lot of people are really bad at this and only want to hear themselves talk. Writer Sarah Miller, in The Guardian , calls them “non-askers,” a term she borrowed from a friend. And they’re everywhere. In a 2015 Harvard Business Review article , consultants Tom Pohlmann and Neethi Mary Thomas reported that, in an informal poll of more than 200 corporate clients, parents estimated that 70-80% of their kids’ conversations were questions, while adults put the share of questions in their own conversations at just 15-25%. It’s like we lose our inherent curiosity somewhere along the way, and we pay for it in the way we relate to others, or don’t. You don’t have to do much research to see how big of a problem this is becoming, from people lamenting horrid first dates where they can’t get a word in edgewise, to an excruciating lack of self-awareness from people in the working world who just… won’t. stop. talking! Asking good questions: The original party trick. Photo credit: Stephen Coles/Flickr Why is this mind-numbingly simple advice so hard to follow? In Quiet: The Power of Introverts in a World That Can’t Stop Talking , author Susan Cain writes that the idea of “having a good personality” is a pretty modern invention. She says that the Western world transformed at some point from a culture of character to a culture of personality, timed around the rise of salesmen and the corporate world. In that burgeoning culture, being charming, charismatic, and a great storyteller was crucial to your success. We think it makes us impressive to know all the answers, have the best stories, have an anecdote or fun fact to share about every topic. In fact, appearing that way can often be the key to getting ahead at work and making more money. We want to be the one holding court at a party, making guests laugh with our raucous jokes and monologues, because we equate that image with popularity, success, and belonging. When manners beat charisma But it wasn’t always this way. My grandad came from a time, in the old South, where good etiquette and manners were more important than being incredibly charming. In the late 1800s, American etiquette writer Thomas E. Hill advised in guides later collected as The Essential Handbook of Victorian Etiquette: “Do not aspire to be a great storyteller. An inveterate teller of long stories becomes very tiresome. To tell one or two witty, short, new stories, appropriate to the occasion, is about all that one person should inflict upon the company.” Etiquette of the era also dictated not bragging about your connections or accomplishments, and not using highfalutin words to sound smarter than you really are. Some funny ones include parents not telling too many stories about their kids (preach!) and avoiding using too many puns. Now, my grandad didn’t exactly grow up in the Victorian era, more like the Great Depression, but you can get a sense of how our priorities have changed since 1900 to today. There were a lot of things about that time period in the United States that weren’t so great, but that emphasis on making other people feel comfortable and heard in social settings, instead of advancing your own status and standing, would be a welcome return. Luckily, it’s easy to do it even today. Just ask a question, literally any question, and you’ll already be doing way better than most people. They don’t call them the Greatest Generation for nothing! This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post My Greatest Generation grandad had one rule to never run out of things to say in conversation appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Η Celia, μια γνωστική επιστήμονας που δημοσιεύει στο Instagram ως @celiaonpsychology, διάλεξε ένα ποίημα του Robert Frost που δεν είχε διαβάσει ποτέ, «Nothing Gold Can Stay» και ξεκίνησε να απομνημονεύσει και τις 40 λέξεις του σε περίπου δύο λεπτά. Αλλά αντί να διαβάζει τις γραμμές ξανά και ξανά, πέρασε νοερά μέσα από το διαμέρισμά της. Η τεχνική ονομάζεται Μέθοδος Τόπων,…
items.descriptionOriginal: Celia, a cognitive scientist who posts on Instagram as @celiaonpsychology , picked a Robert Frost poem she had never read, “ Nothing Gold Can Stay ,” and set out to memorize all 40 words of it in about two minutes. But instead of reading the lines over and over, she mentally walked through her apartment. The technique is called the Method of Loci , and it works by hanging each item you need to remember on a physical spot in a place you know well. Celia started at her front door and moved inward, assigning a visual image to every word in the poem and leaving it somewhere specific. A green sofa in the living room held the word “green.” For “hardest,” she pictured a woman holding a diamond. A color gradient stood in for “hue,” and a mother holding a baby represented “hold.” View this post on Instagram Once every word had an image and a spot, she closed her eyes and walked the route again, reading the poem back off the furniture. She got 35 of the 40 words on the first pass. The method is roughly 2,500 years old, and its origin story is grim. Credit usually goes to the Greek poet Simonides of Ceos , who stepped out of a banquet hall just before the roof collapsed on everyone inside. The bodies were crushed beyond recognition, and Simonides could identify them because he remembered exactly where each guest had been sitting. View this post on Instagram Roman orators later built the technique into their formal training. Cicero used it to deliver long speeches without notes, and the Sherlock Holmes stories popularized the term “mind palace” for modern audiences. Unlike most study hacks that circulate on social media, the method of loci holds up in controlled trials. When researchers scanned the brains of ten of the world’s top memory competitors, it turned out that nine were using the technique, and their brains lit up in regions associated with spatial navigation. A 2021 meta-analysis by Twomey and Kroneisen in the Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology pooled 13 randomized trials and found a medium effect on recall. A separate 2021 study in Science Advances found that six weeks of training produced longer-lasting memory than working-memory training or no intervention at all. View this post on Instagram The technique isn’t 100% effortless, as the video’s comments quickly pointed out. “I wonder why do so much; just read. [Do] it 3 times and memorize. This method seems more difficult,” one viewer wrote . For a short eight-line poem, that commenter has a point: setting up dozens of mental images takes work, but the method makes more sense for longer material that has to come back in a fixed order. That’s why you’ll see it show up in medical school, in speech preparation, and at the World Memory Championship . It’s also reusable. Once you no longer need the poem, the same apartment can hold something else. You can follow Celia (@celiaonpsychology) for more psychology-related content. The post She memorized a poem she’d never read in two minutes, using a trick from ancient Greece appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οικονομική αγοραστής παντοπωλείου μοιράζεται μια λιτή γιορτή 50 δολαρίων για την Ημέρα των Ευχαριστιών για να ταΐσει την τετραμελή οικογένειά της
items.titleOriginal: Budget grocery shopper shares frugal $50 Thanksgiving feast to feed her family of four
items.description: Φέτος, το μέσο κόστος ενός γεύματος για την Ημέρα των Ευχαριστιών θα κοστίσει περίπου 90 δολάρια, σύμφωνα με την εταιρεία συμβούλων PwC. Και με τις τιμές των τροφίμων να συνεχίζουν να αυξάνονται λόγω του πληθωρισμού, η εξοικονόμηση χρημάτων σε μια μεγάλη γιορτή των Ευχαριστιών μπορεί να είναι πιο δύσκολη από ποτέ. Ευτυχώς, η μαμά και η οικονομική blogger Julia Pacheco δημιούργησε έναν προϋπολογισμό 50 $ για παντοπωλεία για την Ημέρα των Ευχαριστιών χρησιμοποιώντας τον Wal…
items.descriptionOriginal: This year, the average cost of a Thanksgiving meal will cost about $90, according to consulting firm PwC . And with food prices continuing to rise due to inflation, saving money on a great Thanksgiving feast may be more difficult than ever. Thankfully, mom and budget food blogger Julia Pacheco has created a $50 Thanksgiving grocery budget using Walmart groceries to feed her family of four not only for Thanksgiving but also for five more meals throughout Thanksgiving week. “Thanksgiving can be so expensive and overwhelming,” Pacheco says in the video’s intro, adding that although a $50 budget is “tight,” she isn’t “sacrificing flavor or taste.” $50 Thanksgiving week menu and grocery list “I know holiday grocery prices can be stressful, so I hope this gives you a few ideas for stretching your Thanksgiving budget a little further,” Pacheco added in the video’s caption. Pacheco was able to create a delicious menu. Thanksgiving feast menu Oven-roasted turkey Deviled eggs Honey-glazed carrots Stuffing Homemade mashed potatoes Turkey gravy Whole berry cranberry sauce Pumpkin crumble dump cake Pacheco also offered viewers an additional five meals to make with leftovers from the original Thanksgiving meal: Leftover meals menu Turkey pot pie Turkey pinto bean burritos Turkey noodle soup Turkey salad sandwiches Turkey cranberry stuffing sandwich She also shared her complete Walmart grocery shopping list, including prices: Thanksgiving grocery shopping list Flour tortillas, $1.98 Egg noodles, $1.78 Loaf of bread, $1.52 Turkey stuffing, 98 cents Can of family-size cream of chicken soup, $1.72 Celery, $2.04 Spice cake mix, $1.94 Canned pumpkin, $1 Can of evaporated milk, $1 Can of cranberry sauce, $1.72 2-pack pie crusts, $1.96 Turkey (84 cents per pound, almost 18-pound turkey with gravy packet), $14.77 Bag of russet potatoes, $1.74 Bag of frozen mixed veggies, 98 cents Dozen eggs, $1.67 Bag of microwavable Spanish-style rice, $1.37 Vanilla ice cream, $3.12 Can of pinto beans, 92 cents Bag of whole carrots, $2.26 Pacheco was under budget, with her items totaling $44.46. Her video includes additional ingredients she already had on hand for the following dishes: Turkey coating 5 tablespoons butter 1 teaspoon pepper 2 teaspoons salt 2 teaspoons celery salt 2-3 teaspoons sage 2 teaspoons thyme Pumpkin crumble dump cake 1 can (15 ounces) pumpkin purée 1 can (12 ounces) evaporated milk 3 large eggs 1/3 cup sugar 1 teaspoon cinnamon (or pumpkin pie spice) 1 box spice cake mix (or yellow cake mix) 3/4 cup unsalted butter (sliced thin) Honey-glazed carrots 2 tablespoons oil 1-2 tablespoons honey 1 teaspoon salt 1 teaspoon pepper Dash of pumpkin pie spice Deviled eggs Yellow mustard Mayonnaise Stuffing 2 ribs celery 2 tablespoons butter Minced onion seasoning Homemade mashed potatoes Half-stick butter Milk Pepper, salt, garlic, sage, and thyme Turkey pinto bean burritos 2 cups turkey Can of pinto beans Bag of microwavable Spanish-style rice Water Taco seasoning to taste Tortillas Turkey noodle soup 6 leftover carrots, sliced 4 ribs leftover celery, sliced 8 1/2 cups chicken broth (from bouillon powder) 2 cups turkey A few spoonfuls of leftover gravy Half a can remaining cream of chicken soup Half a bag egg noodles Cooking the Thanksgiving feast Pacheco starts with the turkey, coating it in the butter mixture for a “flavorful, scrumptious turkey,” before baking it at 325° Fahrenheit. She plans to bake it 15-20 minutes per pound. From there, she moves on to preparing dessert and sides. Pumpkin crumble d ump cake First is the pumpkin crumble dump cake. She mixes all the ingredients together, minus the spice cake mix, and pours in a 9″ x 13″ baking pan. Then she tops the mixture with the spice cake mix that is then topped with the butter slices to create the crumble on top. She bakes it at 350° Fahrenheit for 50 minutes. Deviled eggs and honey-glazed carrots Next, she prepares the deviled eggs. She boils all 12 eggs while she starts prepping the carrots (about half the bag) by slicing and placing them in a parchment-lined baking dish with 2 tablespoons of oil, 1-2 tablespoons honey, 1 teaspoon salt, 1 teaspoon pepper, and a dash of pumpkin pie spice. She bakes it at 350-400° Fahrenheit for about 35 minutes. Once the eggs have cooled, she removes the yolks, adds yellow mustard and mayonnaise to taste, and dashes of salt and pepper. She combines the ingredients and adds the mixture into the hard-boiled egg whites. Stuffing Pacheco slices 2 ribs of celery and puts them in a pan on the stovetop to brown with butter before adding in the stuffing mix. “It adds the extra flavor I think it needs,” she says. Homemade mashed potatoes, gravy, and cranberry sauce Pacheco’s recipe calls for 8 russet potatoes. She peels and chops them and adds the potatoes to a pot of boiling water. Once cooked, she drains them and puts them back in the pot, where she adds milk, butter, and spices before mashing. Next, she prepares the gravy packet from the turkey and removes the whole berry cranberry sauce from the can. Leftover Thanksgiving meals The next day, Pacheco shares how she made each of the leftover meals. Turkey pot pie 2 cups turkey Leftover carrots Leftover stuffing Leftover cranberry sauce (small amount) 3/4 cup frozen mixed vegetables Half a can cream of chicken soup Dash of salt, pepper, minced onion spice, sage, and thyme She mixes together the ingredients for the turkey pot pie. Then she lines a greased pie dish with one of the pre-made pie crusts before adding in the turkey pot pie mixture. Pacheco then covers the pie with the second pre-made crust, poking holes in the top. She bakes at 375° Fahrenheit for about 45 minutes. Turkey pinto bean burritos 2 cups turkey Can of pinto beans Bag of microwavable Spanish-style rice Water Taco seasoning to taste Tortillas Pacheco adds all the ingredients (minus the tortillas) to a pan on her stovetop. She then fills the tortillas with the burrito filling, which amounted to 8 burritos that she recommends freezing. She crisps them up a bit by placing them in a skillet with oil, which gives them “a million times better flavor.” Turkey noodle soup 6 leftover carrots, sliced 4 ribs leftover celery, sliced 8 1/2 cups chicken broth (from bouillon powder) 2 cups turkey A few spoonfuls of leftover gravy Half a can remaining cream of chicken soup Half a bag egg noodles In a soup pot, she combines the carrots and celery to brown with oil. From there, she adds in the chicken broth, turkey, leftover gravy, and remaining cream of chicken soup. She lets the mixture simmer for 15-20 minutes before adding in half a bag of egg noodles and letting it simmer another 10 minutes. Turkey salad sandwiches 2 cups turkey 4 ribs celery, sliced Cranberry sauce Pepper, salt, yellow mustard, and mayonnaise to taste Bread (for sandwich) Next up is making the turkey salad for the sandwiches. Pacheco simply adds all her ingredients to a large mixing bowl. “It’s bursting with flavor,” she says before adding the mixture to slices of bread. Turkey cranberry stuffing sandwich 8 slices bread (for 4 sandwiches) Leftover gravy Leftover mashed potatoes Remaining cranberry sauce Turkey Finally, she prepares these open-faced sandwiches using the remaining ingredients. On each slice of bread, she spreads a bit of gravy before adding a smear of mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, and turkey. She tops each one with another slice of bread and recommends toasting them. The post Budget grocery shopper shares frugal $50 Thanksgiving feast to feed her family of four appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο Wilson Pickett εμφανίστηκε στο σόου του Tom Jones και όταν τραγούδησαν το «Midnight Hour», το δωμάτιο πήρε φωτιά
items.titleOriginal: Wilson Pickett performed on Tom Jones’ show, and when they sang ‘Midnight Hour,’ the room caught fire
items.description: Στα μέσα της δεκαετίας του 1960, ο Ουαλός τραγουδιστής Tom Jones έκανε θύελλα τον κόσμο της μουσικής. Η έντονη φωνή του, το απαλό του στυλ και η μαγνητική του ενέργεια τον έκαναν διεθνή σούπερ σταρ σε μια νύχτα. Δημιούργησε τεράστιες ποπ επιτυχίες και κέρδισε εκατομμύρια θαυμαστές σε όλο τον κόσμο. Δεν έβλαψε αυτό, στην εποχή της βρετανικής εισβολής γεμάτη με νεανικά, αγορίστικα συγκροτήματα, ο Jones b…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the mid-1960s, Welsh powerhouse vocalist Tom Jones took the music world by storm. His booming voice, smooth style, and magnetic energy made him an international superstar overnight. He churned out massive pop hits and won over millions of fans worldwide. It didn’t hurt that, in the British Invasion era filled with youthful, boyish bands, Jones brought a lot of grown-man energy. Like many music stars of that golden age , Jones eventually brought his act to television. He hosted his own variety show, This Is Tom Jones. The weekly format gave him a platform to bring in diverse, brilliant acts. Not content to stay safely inside his pop music bubble , Jones would share the spotlight with everyone, from hard rockers to soul singers. A kid from a Welsh mining town Tom Jones didn’t start life in sequins. He grew up in Pontypridd, a mining town in South Wales. Before fame, he worked construction jobs and even worked in a glove factory. Then came “It’s Not Unusual.” The song hit number one in the U.K. in 1965. Almost overnight, that big baritone belonged to the world. Additional bangers like “What’s New Pussycat?” and the James Bond theme “Thunderball” turned Jones into a bona fide superstar. But he still wanted to share the spotlight with other musical greats. During his 1965 American tour, Jones heard Wilson Pickett’s version of “In the Midnight Hour.” The singer was performing on Hollywood a Go-Go , and his impassioned delivery mesmerized Jones in particular. Five years later, he reached out to Pickett to join him as a musical guest on his variety show. What happened next continues to blow music fans away. Two legendary singers share a single magical stage When Wilson Pickett appears on camera, the energy in the room instantly shifts. The Prattville, Alabama-born singer delivers pure, unadulterated soul as he digs into the song, “Barefootin’.”’ You can see how thrilled Jones is to trade revved-up vocal runs with one of the most powerful, raw voices in American music. The audience is audibly in the pocket for the pair, but “Barefootin’” is only the start of their showstopping performance. The centerpiece is a duet of Pickett’s soul anthem, “In the Midnight Hour.” When vocal powerhouses collide Pickett, whose career began in the Stax Soul scene, growls his verses with unbridled power. Jones meets him step for step in a volley of vocal prowess. Neither singer backs down for a single beat. The emotions are real, and the performance is electrifying. Both performers beam as they take in the crowd and the moment’s excitement. The duo concludes with a cover of The Beatles’ “Hey Jude.” Pickett and Jones dig into the classic hit’s emotions: it’s unpredictable, bold, and feels both immediate and vital. The chemistry between the two men created pure magic on camera. Today, decades after it first aired, footage of their 1970 duet continues to go viral. Millions of music fans still marvel at the incredible vocal gymnastics. It stands as a timeless reminder of what happens when real talent meets deep mutual respect: sparks fly every time. The post Wilson Pickett performed on Tom Jones’ show, and when they sang ‘Midnight Hour,’ the room caught fire appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Amy Poehler is not fazed by getting older. In fact, in a Wall Street Journal interview , she turns the entire concept on its head. Instead of rattling off her ailments and fears, she lists reasons why aging can actually be delightful. It’s often difficult to scroll through social media without being bombarded with ads promising ways to “look and feel” younger. This is nothing new, but since we have more access, it can feel even more intrusive. So when Poehler is asked, “What is something about getting older that has actually made you better at your job?” she gives a splendidly surprising answer. View this post on Instagram ‘You didn’t fall apart’ Wearing a casual black sweater over a bright orange button-down, Poehler perks up and responds, “Oh my God. Getting older is great! Having experience and some wisdom. You have a lot of opportunities where things went badly, and you survived. Like you didn’t fall apart?” Contemplating the “work” part of the question for a second, she adds, “You also didn’t get to realize how you like to work. Who do you like to be around?” She describes the idea of being more flexible with what you thought were core beliefs: “You get a little bit less certain. So your certainty is really important in your 20s and 30s. Like, ‘I always. I never. I hate this. I love this. This is wrong. This is right.’ (It) starts to get a little hazier, and I think that’s a good thing for work because it keeps you more open-minded and curious. And I think less rigid.” Poehler then discusses what some might see as a downside of aging and explains why it’s not necessarily true. “You also get a little more tired. And that’s good too. Because you realize, like, the capacity that you have for things is maybe smaller. But that’s not necessarily a bad thing.” View this post on Instagram Dinner and bedtime? The earlier, the better She shares that there’s nothing wrong with an early dinner or bedtime. “And you start to curate what you care about more. I love an early dinner. I mean, it is almost bedtime for me. What is it, 6:30? We need to be digesting by 6:45. We need to be on a walk.” The journalist jokes, “So we really ruined your schedule today?” Poehler doesn’t bat an eye as she deadpans, “Yeah, I’m gonna be up all night. I’m gonna have to have a cold bologna sandwich and call it a night.” The clip has resonated with viewers, and many in the comments say they feel “seen.” The dinner/sleep element especially connected, with one commenter writing, “The dinner time…absolutely! Lol. I loooooove an early dinner, bed by 8:30. Truly getting older is so freeing. You don’t feel stuck in some box and really come into your own. It’s amazing.” To that point, another adds, “What is the dinner thing? I hate eating late. I hate anything that starts after 7 p.m. Why can’t we just get it done? Be home, showered, robe, bed!” View this post on Instagram Another Instagrammer was struck by Poehler’s mention of being less rigid. “Perhaps the best part of getting older is realizing how much we still don’t know,” they wisely shared. The post Amy Poehler’s celebratory response to ‘getting older’ question deserves a standing ovation appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Τι κάνει τη Scary Music Scary; Ο συνθέτης "Obsession" για τη δημιουργία μιας ταινίας τρόμου δολοφονίας

Ξεκινά ήσυχα, η κάμερα ακολουθεί τη Shelley Duvall καθώς περπατά προς ένα σκιερό δωμάτιο. Τα βήματά της αντηχούν στη σιωπή προτού εισέλθει ένας δυσοίωνος ήχος, σχεδόν σαν παραμορφωμένος λευκός θόρυβος. Ο…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the second half of Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining , there’s an iconic sequence that’s arguably as terrifying as Jack Nicholson’s ax-wielding rampage. It begins quietly, the camera following Shelley Duvall as she walks toward a shadowy room. Her footsteps echo in the silence before an ominous sound creeps in, almost like distorted white noise. The music builds, getting louder and more complex as warped high notes slowly penetrate the din. It’s chaotic, dissonant, deafening, mirroring the emotions on Duvall’s face, until finally, finally — well, we won’t give you any spoilers . “If you watched it on mute, I don’t know if it would feel nearly as scary,” Rock Burwell told Nice News of the classic flick. Burwell composed the score for this year’s breakout indie horror film, Obsession , which raked in $500 million-plus off a $750,000 budget, making it the highest-grossing movie ever produced for under $1 million. The Los Angeles-based composer recognizes how essential music is to evoking emotion in filmgoers, and his eerie orchestration played an outsize role in Obsession’s success. “What just generally has always drawn me to music in the first place is its ability to influence how we feel,” he said. But what exactly makes scary music scary? We may all have some general idea of the characteristics of creepy music — the crescendo of staccato strings in Psycho ’s shower scene comes to mind — but the way in which a score achieves its effect varies greatly. There are certain common elements, however, that lend themselves to disconcerting an audience. Subverting Expectations For Obsession , Burwell — after discussions with writer-director Curry Barker — chose a nontraditional approach, opting to subtly discomfit viewers through dreamy, nostalgic melodies, slightly pitch-bending his notes and drenching everything in reverb. “It was fun to explore not coming in with these really harsh, interval, screechy-sounding kind of things that you hear in a lot of horror movies,” he explained, “but actually coming from something that feels a bit more warm and almost comforting. But the way it moves and is undulating underneath is very — it kind of gets under your skin a little bit more.” Composer Katy Jarzebowski , who recently scored the award-winning documentary Gaslit featuring Jane Fonda, has been working in the industry for over 20 years. She noted that today’s savvy audiences are well-versed in the language of film. The key to unsettling them, then, is to present a musical choice they don’t necessarily understand or expect. “If you give them something that they know and love, then it kind of takes that feeling of discomfort away,” she explained, adding: “[When filmmakers] don’t give them something that they expect, it becomes uncomfortable.” Tension Tension is the heart of any horror film, and a good one typically leaves viewers on tenterhooks throughout. To that end, Burwell noted that the descending melodies and drawn-out cues he used can cause audiences to feel as though they’re suspended, waiting for a resolution that never comes. “Everything is very, like, ambient and long, and it’s slow moving,” he said. “I think that the pace of it really allows those feelings to sit in a bit longer.” He added that he’s heard from fans that the sweet-yet-tainted score had them feeling “very comforted, but at the same time, feeling kind of bad or that there’s something missing or that there’s yearning.” Jarzebowski agreed with the idea of holding out on viewers. “It’s a lot about where you choose to come in or where you choose to hold back,” she said. “You know, a lot of times [it’s] not giving that kind of pillow for the audience to land on to remind them that they’re in a movie in the first place.” In the Studio Pete Horner is an Emmy-winning sound designer and re-recording mixer at Skywalker Sound (who also happens to be married to Jarzebowski). He pointed out that the terror conveyed through a horror movie’s sound isn’t merely from the music itself. Foley is the art of creating sound effects in a studio — things like footsteps or a door creaking — and Horner said it can be used to great effect for inducing fear in quiet scenes. “By accentuating those things, it kind of draws you closer to the action, and it makes you feel uncomfortable because you shouldn’t be able to hear that,” he explained, adding: “It mimics what happens when you are scared, which is that you become hyperaware of your surroundings. And when you’re not scared, you probably don’t hear the footsteps at all, even though they are happening in the space you’re in. But if you are scared, every little tiny sound has huge meaning.” Additionally, gradually removing the ambient background noise (called “room tone”) from a scene can be extremely disconcerting. “It’s something you want to use sparingly in a movie, but if you pull out of all of the ambiences, the effect that it has is the audience will hold their breath,” Horner said. “Because they’re listening, they’re trying to hear into the sound, and there’s nothing there. And it’s a very scary feeling.” Working With the Cinematography It’s typical for musicians to score to picture, meaning they create the music as they watch the film. But sometimes, the two arts inform each other more equally. In Obsession , Burwell sent early cues to Barker while he and director of photography Taylor Clemons were coming up with the shot list. Barker later told Burwell that playing the music on set really helped establish the mood they were going for. Likewise, watching Clemons’ claustrophobic cinematography influenced Burwell’s choices for the score. “We kind of leaned on the darkness, like, there’s not much high frequency information in the music, and there’s not a whole lot of light in a lot of these scenes, too,” Burwell said. “I’ve kind of referred to it as a lot of the score feeling like a lead blanket or something like that. Like, it’s just really heavy. And I think the cinematography really informed that for me.” Experimentation Starting with what’s considered the first-ever horror flick (a three-minute silent French film from 1896 titled The Haunted Castle ) to the dozens coming out in 2027 , the genre is a confirmed favorite of moviegoers. Call it sublimation or call it masochism, but people like to be scared. And that means composers have ample opportunity — and one could say the imperative — to get creative. “Horror is a great place for composers, especially to experiment with different things because a lot of times, you’re trying to create a fear that someone doesn’t know yet,” Jarzebowski said, adding: “We already have Psycho , we have Stranger Things , we have [horror filmmaker and composer John] Carpenter — all this horror language that we’ve created. So you already know what to be scared of. So there’s always room for, like, ‘OK, what else can we do to make it even scarier? What haven’t they heard yet?’”

items.descriptionOriginal: What spooks you? A mysterious thud downstairs in the middle of the night, spotting a spider on your pillow, and feeling something brush against your leg in the sea are among the top 10 things that make Brits scream, according to a recent survey of 2,000 adults in the U.K. Yet despite being quick to shriek, the nation appears to embrace the fun side of fear, with 84% of respondents saying scary experiences are more likely to end in laughter than panic when shared with others. More than half also confirmed enjoying spooky thrills in a group setting tends to leave them laughing, particularly when watching horror films, riding roller coasters, or braving a haunted attraction. SWNS According to psychologist Kimberley Wilson, there’s a scientific reason these scary experiences can feel surprisingly enjoyable, something she’s dubbed the “Shared Shriek Effect.” “When we watch something scary, our bodies respond as if we’re facing a threat. Our heart rate increases, adrenaline rises, and our attention sharpens,” she told SWNS. “The difference is that our brains know we’re actually safe, which allows us to experience that physical rush as excitement rather than fear.” Wilson added: “When we share that experience with other people, whether we’re jumping, screaming, or laughing together, it can create a genuine sense of connection. The scream itself also helps release the tension that’s been building up, which is why laughter so often follows.” There are benefits beyond the thrill, too, with a quarter saying that being scared offers an escape from everyday life, while 24% see it as a healthy emotional release. Nearly 1 in 5 of those polled also believe it acts as an instant stress reliever. The research was done via OnePoll and commissioned by M&M’s to mark the launch of the candy brand’s new “ Screaming Service ,” encouraging people to swap streaming for screaming this Halloween. “We think Halloween isn’t really about being scared, it’s about screaming together,” said Georgia Woodward, a senior brand manager at M&M’s. “Our ‘Screaming Service’ celebrates those moments across the month of Halloween when everyone jumps at the same scenes, hides behind a cushion, and ends up laughing together about it afterwards.” Top 10 Things That Make Brits Shriek SWNS 1. Someone unexpectedly jumping out at you as a prank 2. Hearing a knock at the window when it’s dark 3. Hearing a mysterious thud downstairs in the night 4. Missing a step at the bottom of the stairs 5. Spotting a spider on your pillow 6. Feeling something brush against your leg in the sea 7. Seeing a mouse dart across a room 8. Being caught off guard by a spooky film twist 9. Someone unexpectedly shouting “boo!” 10. Walking face-first into a cobweb This article was originally written by Zara Zubeidi for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Sometimes, it can feel like half of parenting is repeating yourself over and over again, asking your child to brush their teeth or take a dish from the living room to the sink. It’s exhausting and makes you feel like a nag. Don’t you wish there was a simple way to make your kids listen the first time? Dr. Rebecca Kennedy , aka “Dr. Becky,” is a clinical psychologist and founder and CEO of Good Inside who says she has a quick way to make your kids more cooperative and less rude. She’s also the author of the #1 New York Times bestseller Good Inside , and her platform now has more than 100,000 paying subscribers, according to Fortune . Talk about killing two soul-crushing birds with one parenting stone. Dr. Becky has said she got into psychology after struggling with anorexia as a teenager. The 15-second question to ask “Okay, no matter how old your kid is, you can use this 15-second tip to decrease rudeness and increase cooperation,” she says in a TikTok video she posted in April 2024. “Find your child today and ask them this question. ‘Hey, I was just wondering, what could I do better as your parent?’” A mom and son talk on the couch. Photo credit: Canva The psychologist says that even if the child gives a random or impractical answer such as “Let me stay up ’til midnight” or “I’d like to eat macaroni and cheese for breakfast, lunch and dinner,” parents should just listen. In her view, simply listening can change your child’s behavior. She says we should also ask more questions to further the conversation: “Tell me more. What would that be like?” @drbeckyatgoodinside Want to improve your relationship with your kid in less than 15 seconds? Watch this reel for a quick-win strategy. The best part: When we use strategies like this in calm moments, we reduce the frequency of difficult moments with our kids. Of course, I’m a realist… I know you need in-the-moment strategies too! Cue: My Conquering Problem Behaviors Workshop. You’ll get an entire toolbox of in-the-moment and outside-the-moment strategies for reducing outbursts and strengthening your bond with your kid. Learn more in the link in bio! ♬ original sound – Dr. Becky | Psychologist “I mean, imagine your boss coming to you randomly and asking how they could be a better manager to you. Just by asking the question and listening,” she continued. Dr. Becky says that asking our kids how we’re doing as parents communicates three essential ideas: “I care about you. I respect you. I’m invested in this relationship.” This type of questioning builds a connection with a child that can spill over into other behaviors. “You’re building connection. And with more connection always comes more cooperation,” she ends the video. Why listening builds cooperation The big takeaway from the video is that when we enhance our connection with our kids, they may be less likely to disobey or be rude because they feel heard and respected, so there’s no need to act out. Dr. Becky’s tip isn’t backed by a study of its own, but it fits with research on parenting styles, which has found that kids with behavior problems are more likely to improve over time when parents adopt authoritative practices, meaning warmth and two-way communication paired with clear expectations. They will also return that respect by listening to you when you have a request, such as taking out the trash or putting down their phone and coming to dinner. Some people in the comments got funny responses when they asked their kids what they could improve. “I asked my 5yr old. I got a mildly scathing look and she said ‘erm, maybe try and burn dinner less next time?’” one parent wrote. “My 5 yo told me to look better and get a haircut,” another added. Dr. Becky’s quick question is a great way for parents to strengthen their relationships when things are going well instead of trying to forge connections during conflict. It’s a great reminder that even when parenting, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. Dr. Becky sums up the importance of prevention in her TikTok caption: “When we use strategies like this in calm moments, we reduce the frequency of difficult moments with our kids,” she wrote. This article originally appeared two years ago. It has been updated. The post Psychologist shares 15-second trick to make kids of any age less rude and more cooperative appeared first on Upworthy .

Αλλά όταν σχολιάζετε ακόμη περισσότερο, η γλώσσα γίνεται…
items.descriptionOriginal: Language is fascinating. The way humans have come up with literally thousands of languages to communicate with one another, the grammatical structures we’ve concocted, the fact that we learn our native tongues so naturally, and how powerful words can be are all testaments to how cool language is. But when you drill down even further, language gets even cooler, and in ways that most of us aren’t even aware of. Linguist and self-professed “etymology nerd” Adam Aleksic shared a video on TikTok explaining how many common phrases we use for thinking directly reference walking. We often use metaphors in our speech, of course, but there are many that we likely don’t even recognize as metaphors. Once you hear this, you can’t unhear it He starts with “by the way,” which literally means being next to the way, or the path we’re supposed to be on. It indicates that we’re taking a mental detour from the path we were supposed to be on to introduce something unrelated. On the other hand, when we’re talking about something that is actually on the path we’re meant to be on, we say, “of course,” which literally means “of the path.” “We use this metaphor all the time when we say, ‘you’re on track’ or ‘you’re way off,’ literally implying that you’re not where you should be on the ‘path’ of thinking,” Aleksic says, explaining that there’s a greater metaphor at play here that “thinking is walking.” Once you see some examples, it becomes so clear. Our minds “race” or “wander,” our thoughts “stray,” and we “arrive” at conclusions. “All this relies on physical motion, even though your mind is stationary,” says Aleksic. “But it’s from that idea (that thoughts can walk) that we can then go ahead and make statements about our own cognition. Like how I just used ‘from,’ originally a preposition for motion, and ‘go ahead’ to indicate continuation. Once you know thoughts can walk, you can ‘follow’ them down ‘a line of thinking’ until you ‘come to’ a resolution.” Here are a few more you’ll recognize Even a saying as common as “Way to go!” is a metaphor indicating that you are on the correct path. Once you start thinking about it, it’s easy to come up with many more examples of how we conceptualize thinking as walking: “Let’s circle back.” “Walk me through your thinking.” “I’m backtracking here.” “The thought crossed my mind.” “No way.” “Let’s move on.” Other languages do the same thing Some commenters shared that their languages use similar metaphors: “In Norwegian you can say ‘du er helt på bærtur’ when someone is way off, and it means that you are on a berry trip, specifically blueberry trip.” “In Czech, you say btw as ‘mimochodem’, while mimo means outside and chodem means a step or a walk, so literally meaning by the walk.” “En passant in french is the same way. It’s like ‘I passed near this thought’ while on my way to another thought.” True to form, Aleksic even has a video commenting on comments : There’s something to be said for “thinking is walking” even beyond the metaphorical way we describe our thoughts. Many of the world’s greatest thinkers were also obsessive walkers . Science backs this up, too In 2014, Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz of Stanford University conducted a foundational series of four experiments involving 176 college students and other adults to see if walking had any effect on different types of thinking. In one test, they had some people walk outside and others walk on a treadmill facing a blank wall to see if the environment made a difference. On brainstorming tasks, it mostly didn’t. Wherever people walked, they came up with more creative ideas than those who sat or were pushed in a wheelchair, and creative output rose by an average of 60%. Participants consistently did better on tests of divergent thinking, such as thinking of alternate uses for common objects, and walking outside produced the most novel, high-quality analogies. The boost did not extend to convergent thinking, where there is a single right answer. “Thinking is walking” and walking can also help us think. Photo credit: Canva “Incorporating physical activity into our lives is not only beneficial for our hearts but our brains as well,” Oppezzo said . “This research suggests an easy and productive way to weave it into certain work activities.” Could we perhaps say, “walking is thinking” in addition to “thinking is walking”? A 2021 study of Japanese young adults found that regular walking was associated with more original responses on alternate uses tests, which measure divergent thinking, though not with convergent thinking. So it appears at least some types of thinking are enhanced by walking. A recent meta-analysis of 23 studies in PLOS ONE found a large effect on divergent thinking but no effect on convergent thinking. Which, of course, makes it all the more fun that we use so many walking metaphors to describe our thoughts. You can follow Adam Aleksic for more on TikTok here or check out his book, Algospeak: How Social Media Is Transforming the Future of Language , here . This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Linguist clearly demonstrates how ‘thinking is walking’ in English and it’s just so cool appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Isn’t it wild to think that spies are actually real? Governments all over the world send secret agents to other countries to steal information or conduct missions. The key element that makes a spy, of course, is the secretive nature of their work. They go undercover, sometimes even wearing disguises, and carry out their missions without attracting attention. That means they’re masters of psychology and social science rather than combat and weaponry. In a revealing interview with Steven Bartlett on his “Diary of a CEO” podcast, former Secret Service Special Agent Evy Poumpouras shared how to get people to do what you want them to do. The key, according to Poumpouras, is to understand what motivates them. Once you know the psychological framework behind what makes them tick, you can persuade them to behave as you like. Poumpouras was a co-host of Bravo TV’s “Spy Games” competition series and author of “ Becoming Bulletproof: Protect Yourself, Read People, Influence Situations, and Live Fearlessly .” She served in the Secret Service’s Presidential Protective Division for President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama and protected George W. Bush, Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush. Her secret to getting people to listen Poumpouras says that to get a “good read” on someone, it’s essential to listen. “The biggest mistake people make is they talk a lot,” Poumpouras said in the video clip. “Steven, if I’m doing all the talking and you’re doing all the listening, you’re learning everything about me. You’re learning about what I care about, my values, my belief systems, getting a good read on me and I’m learning nothing about you.” The former Secret Service Agent says that you should listen to determine the subject’s motivational mindset. Are they motivated by money, sex, admiration, status, freedom, relationships, or safety? “Everybody’s motivated by something different. But I have to hear you and pay attention to you to understand what that is. Everybody’s purpose is different,” she continued. “If you give people enough space, they will reveal themselves to you.” To be clear, Poumpouras isn’t in the business of helping people trick others. Instead, she hopes the techniques she teaches will accomplish this: “Increase your self-confidence, your self-worth, and your ability to trust and believe in yourself.” The commenters on TikTok loved the advice: “People are so interested in themselves and want to talk about themselves… We give our power away by talking.” “Changed my life when I was told to stop filling the silence” “As a parent, I needed this reminder too.” Yes, the parents came out in full force to support Poumpouras’ tip. Perhaps no one, other than espionage experts, better understands the importance of learning how to get other people to do things without threats and violence. (OK, sometimes there are threats). View this post on Instagram It’s also a wonderful tactic because your subject will have no idea they are part of a manipulation because they are the ones doing the talking. It’s nearly impossible to give yourself away when you’re sitting in silence. Understanding what motivates people is essential when protecting the safety of the nation’s most important assets and dealing with shady, dangerous people. But it’s not only useful for spies and double agents. Why it works outside the spy world This so-called “trick” can also benefit the layperson by giving us a framework to understand people better. Knowing what motivates someone is very important, whether you’re on a date, in a business deal, or in a leadership role at work. It’s also very important when raising children or training an animal. The data agrees. In a well-known study led by Wharton organizational psychologist Adam Grant, university fundraisers who briefly met a student who had benefited from their work spent 142% more time on the phone and brought in 171% more revenue than a control group. In other words, people are much more likely to go above and beyond for tasks they feel emotionally invested in. So, if you want people to do things that benefit you, sure you can pay them or convince them that it’s in their best interest, but you’ll have far better luck if you appeal to their core principles and desires. To do that, you first have to listen and find out what they are. Know what drives you, too Understanding your personal motivators is also essential for making the best choices in life. It helps us determine which actions will be genuinely beneficial. It’s also a great way to ensure that we are involved with people, organizations, and activities for the right reasons. In other words, digging into someone else’s (and your own) core beliefs and motivation can be used for good! Not just protecting state secrets and preventing assassinations. Productivity consultant Ashley Janssen says the key to understanding your motives is knowing your values. “When you know what you value, you can identify how an activity or goal will support and foster those values,” Janssen writes . “When you decide to try something, consider whether it’s what you think you should want to do or what someone else has said you should do. Those conditions are often not enough to sustain a behavior or activity. It’s hard to keep moving forward on something that you don’t really care about or are not invested in.” This article originally appeared two years ago. It has been updated. The post Former Secret Service Agent reveals ingenious ‘spy trick’ to gain the upper hand in any conversation appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Μια κυριακάτικη τηλεοπτική σειρά του 1995 γίνεται viral επειδή κανείς δεν πιστεύει ότι υπήρχε στην πραγματικότητα
items.titleOriginal: A 1995 Sunday TV show lineup is going viral because nobody believes it actually existed
items.description: Το έτος ήταν 1995. Το διαδίκτυο όπως το ξέρετε σήμερα ήταν ακόμα στα σπάργανα. Αλλά αν ξεφυλλίζατε τον Οδηγό TV ή την τοπική εφημερίδα σας, μπορεί να έχετε βρει μια διαφήμιση για την εναρκτήρια σειρά του The WB την Κυριακή το βράδυ. Όταν εμφανίστηκε στο X τον Ιούλιο, αυτή η κλασική έντυπη διαφήμιση τηγάνισε περισσότερα από λίγα εγκεφαλικά κύτταρα. Διαθέτει ένα πλέγμα από χαμογελαστό αστέρι…
items.descriptionOriginal: The year was 1995 . The internet as you know it today was still in its infancy. But if you flipped through TV Guide or your local newspaper, you might have stumbled across an ad for The WB’s inaugural Sunday night fall lineup . When it surfaced on X in July, this classic print ad fried more than a few brain cells. It features a grid of smiling stars hawking sitcoms that most people have never heard of . And after racking up more than 150K views, many in the X thread insisted there was no way this marketing poster was real. It must be AI-generated, they said. There’s not a single show from this 1995 The WB lineup I remember. The series “Simon” in particular feels like it never existed. pic.twitter.com/Jpkj97H1AA — Valerie D'Orazio (@TheVallyD) July 26, 2026 “Harland Williams and Jason Bateman had a show together?” asked one X user. “That lineup gave me a full dose of the Mandela Effect .” It’s not a glitch in the matrix ; this moment in pop culture history definitely happened. Before The WB became the sacred home of teen angst and brooding vampires, the network had to kiss a lot of frogs to find the right fit for its audience. Michigan J. Frog included. How The WB got off the ground The WB began in the wake of Fox becoming America’s fourth major network. Warner Bros. Television Studios was already supplying the major broadcasters with dramas and comedies, but studio heads figured it was time to have a platform of their own. When the channel first premiered in January 1995, its Wednesday night lineup featured edgier fare like The Wayans Bros. This was Shawn and Marlon Wayans’ shot at the big time after being featured on Fox’s In Living Color . It was paired with The Parent ‘Hood , a family sitcom from Robert Townsend (who you may know from Hollywood Shuffle and The Bear ). Also on that night was a provocative new comedy from the co-creator of Married… with Children . Titled Unhappily Ever After , it featured a talking stuffed animal that only one character could hear, voiced by none other than Bobcat Goldthwait. Each of these shows lasted five seasons, eventually shifting to other nights as The WB expanded its weekly programming. The sole canceled series from that launch lineup was a soap opera parody called Muscle . The series started with a “Who Shot J.R.?”-style murder mystery over the death of Adam West’s character and ended with every character succumbing to death by gunshot. It was canceled before its first season was over, making it the first series The WB ever canceled. The lost sitcom era that sounds like pure fiction Later that year, The WB expanded to Sundays in September, building a three-hour block around Pinky and the Brain and reruns of the Mowry twins’ show Sister, Sister, which the network had rescued when ABC canceled it after one season. The block paired this known quantity with other TGIF-like sitcoms that network executives thought viewers would want to tune in for the rest of the night. Kirk (starring Growing Pains teen heartthrob Kirk Cameron) had a Full House -like premise, while Simon ‘s brother-duo comedy featured a personality-clash setup à la Perfect Strangers . Cleghorne! , meanwhile, was a workplace comedy starring former Saturday Night Live cast member Ellen Cleghorne, while First Time Out was in the vein of Friends and Living Single . These were shows starring household names like Bateman, Cameron, and future sitcom staple Leah Remini. And yet no one remembers them. At least not on a wide scale, which is precisely why so many on social media are calling the lineup fake. Out of these four shows, only Kirk was renewed. It was later canceled early in its sophomore season. None of them amassed enough episodes to land in syndication, so they quietly vanished. They left behind little more than a few paltry Wikipedia entries and a bunch of confused social media replies. How the weirdest lineup led to beating the odds What makes this forgotten television artifact so fascinating isn’t just that it happened. It’s that it paved the way for what came next. Starting in 1997 and continuing into the early 2000s, The WB premiered a group of dramas that still have a massive cult following today. Series like Buffy the Vampire Slayer , Dawson’s Creek , Charmed , and Gilmore Girls , just to name a few. While those WB comedy pioneers may seem out of place next to these landmark shows, sitcoms starring Jamie Foxx, Reba McEntire, and Steve Harvey would soon run on the network for years. This entire viral episode is an intriguing reminder of the chaotic Wild West days of 1990s television, a time when upstart channels threw anything at the wall just to see what would stick. So no, your eyes aren’t playing tricks on you. It isn’t another algorithmic hallucination, either. That glorious, baffling Sunday night lineup of 1995 really happened, singing-and-dancing frog logo and all. This article originally appeared in July. It has been updated. The post A 1995 Sunday TV show lineup is going viral because nobody believes it actually existed appeared first on Upworthy .

Η Klebsiella pneumoniae είναι ένα επικίνδυνο βακτήριο που σκοτώνει χιλιάδες βρέφη σε χώρες χαμηλού και μεσαίου εισοδήματος κάθε χρόνο και είναι ο μεγαλύτερος δολοφόνος παιδιών παγκοσμίως. Τέτοιες λοιμώξεις μπορεί να είναι δύσκολες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have discovered that vaccinating mouse mothers transfers antibodies that defend vulnerable newborns against Klebsiella pneumoniae . Klebsiella pneumoniae is a dangerous bacterium that kills thousands of infants in low- and middle-income countries each year and is the leading killer of children globally. Such infections can be difficult to treat due to the bacterium’s growing resistance to antibiotics and there is currently no vaccine available to prevent infection. The study in Science Advances points to a promising new strategy for protecting vulnerable infants from the drug-resistant superbug by harnessing maternal immunity. “ Klebsiella pneumoniae is a serious threat to newborns who have not yet developed their own immune defenses,” says the study’s senior author, David A. Rosen, an associate professor of pediatrics and of molecular microbiology at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. “Our study shows that maternal immunization can effectively bridge that critical window of vulnerability, giving newborns the protection they need right from birth.” K. pneumoniae is a big problem around the world, especially in the hospital where it can cause pneumonia and other infections among adults and children. In low- and middle-income countries, where children often get exposed to the bacterium in their environment, it drives severe bacterial blood infections, known as sepsis. Because K. pneumoniae is increasingly resistant to standard antibiotics, doctors are often left without effective medicines to treat such infections. The Rosen team collaborated with the lab of Drew Schwartz, an assistant professor of pediatrics, to model K. pneumoniae sepsis in newborn mice that mimics the infection seen in children and asked if vaccinating a pregnant mouse would prevent infection in pups. Female mice were immunized at the time of mating and then again once or twice during pregnancy. The vaccine targets two of the most dangerous types of K. pneumoniae —known as K1 and K2—and was developed by Omniose, a St. Louis-based startup. Rosen had previously published findings that show the vaccine is effective in preventing K. pneumoniae infection in adult mice that can progress to life-threatening liver, respiratory tract, bloodstream, and other infections. Two weeks after birth, the young mice were exposed to lethal doses of the bacteria, either the K1 or K2 type. Of the two-week-old mouse pups from unvaccinated mothers, 0% infected with the K1 type and less than 35% with the K2 type survived. In contrast, of the young mice from vaccinated mothers, more than 80% infected with either type survived. Whether the mother received two or three doses of the vaccine did not impact survival. The researchers drew blood weekly from the young mice starting on their day of birth and continuing up to six weeks of life. They also collected breast milk from lactating mice. They found high concentrations of vaccine-specific antibodies in both the milk of vaccinated mothers and their newborn mice over the course of the study. “Mice that were never immunized themselves are highly protected from a lethal infection just from the durable antibodies transferred to them from their mother,” explains first author Paeton Wantuch, a staff scientist in the Rosen lab. The researchers are now testing updated vaccines designed to shield against multiple strains of the superbug found across the globe. “This study presents the first evidence that giving moms a vaccine could be an effective strategy for protecting their babies against these severe infections,” says Rosen. “And it also has established a practical model that we can now use to test therapies and vaccines that will bring us one step closer to human clinical trials with the ultimate goal of impacting global health.” This work was supported by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Gates Foundation, and the Washington University Department of Pediatrics. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official view of the NIH, the Gates Foundation or other funders. Competing Interest Statement: Robinson LS, Darwech I, Knoot CJ, and Harding CM have a financial stake in Omniose, a for-profit entity developing bioconjugate vaccines using patented technology reflected in the data presented in this and other published manuscripts. Source: Washington University in St. Louis The post Can a vaccine for moms protect infants from a deadly superbug? appeared first on Futurity .

Αν και μπορεί να μην είναι νωρίς στις 6 π.μ., έχουν πολλές μοναδικές δυνάμεις και χαρακτηριστικά προσωπικότητας που πηγάζουν από τον χρονοτύπο τους που ευνοεί τη νύχτα. Αλλά το να είσαι κουκουβάγια είναι κάτι…
items.descriptionOriginal: Night owls are people who come alive at night . According to UCLA Health , 30% of the world’s population identifies as night owls, people who are most productive at night. While they may not be early birds at 6 a.m., they have many unique strengths and personality traits that stem from their night-favoring chronotype . But being a night owl is sometimes stereotyped as lazy , which mental health experts say is not true. “Being a night owl is not laziness, and it’s not a lack of discipline,” Sandra Kushnir , LMFT, a licensed therapist and founder and CEO of Meridian Counseling, tells Upworthy. Instead, she explains that many night owls are born that way—they carry a genetic variant that inclines them to stay up late. “A big part of chronotype is biological, and forcing a night owl into a 5 a.m. routine usually backfires,” she adds. For night owls, Kushnir explains that their real work is protecting their sleep—getting enough of it, keeping the wind-down consistent, and building a schedule that fits their natural circadian rhythm. “When night owls stop fighting their wiring and start working with it, their mood and relationships often improve too,” notes Kushnir. Personality traits of night owls Night owls have specific personality traits that set them apart from early birds. Here are six interesting things about them: Personality trait No. 1: They’re curious and open to new experiences “Research has found some association between evening chronotypes and openness to experience,” Somer Welch , MPSA, MSW, LCSW, a licensed clinical social worker trained in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) and founder of Resurgence Therapy PLLC, tells Upworthy. She explains that for night owls, the night offers a chance to expand their minds without the interruptions of everyday life. “You start looking up a recipe at 11 p.m., and before you know it, you’re reading about some obscure historical event that has absolutely nothing to do with dinner,” she adds. “There’s something wonderful about having the freedom to get lost in whatever catches your attention.” Personality trait No. 2: They’re willing to take risks Night owls may be bigger risk takers. “There’s also a link to a greater willingness to take risks,” Laurie Groh , MS, LPC, SAS, a licensed professional counselor and owner of Shoreside Therapies in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, tells Upworthy. She explains that some research suggests night owls tend to take greater risks due to higher levels of testosterone and cortisol than non-night owls, which may contribute to this behavior. Personality trait No. 3: They have a looser relationship with routine When it comes to sticking to a schedule, night owls may not follow one to a “T,” Stephanie Levitt , MA, LPC, NCC, founder and Licensed Professional Counselor of Pathways Counseling Services, tells Upworthy. “Night owls tend to score lower on conscientiousness, the Big Five personality trait that includes characteristics like being organized and punctual,” she shares, adding that night owls therefore likely may have a “looser relationship with schedules and routines.” Personality trait No. 4: They’re independent thinkers “Night owls tend to be comfortable doing their own thing,” says Kushnir. “Choosing to be most alive when the rest of the house is asleep says something about a person who doesn’t need the group’s schedule to feel okay.” She adds that many night owls do their best thinking when nobody needs anything from them, and that “quiet stretch is where they recharge.” Personality trait No. 5: They’re novelty-seeking “Other studies have shown that novelty seeking is also a tendency of night owls,” says Groh. “They might be drawn to things that are new or stimulating. And sometimes, part of what keeps somebody awake is being interested in something.” Personality Trait No. 6: They’re emotionally deep, and sometimes a little restless Night owls also may be more self-reflective. “In my work as a therapist, I notice that night owls often process their emotions at night,” Kushnir explains. “The day is busy, so the feelings wait until it’s quiet. That can make them reflective and self-aware, but it can also mean overthinking at 1 AM. It’s not a character flaw, it’s just when the mind finally has room.” The post Night owls aren’t lazy. Psychologists say they have 6 unique personality traits that set them apart. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have developed muscle actuators that flex strongly enough to enable small robots to jump, swim, walk, and grasp. Lab-grown skeletal muscle tissue can contract, but the movement is often so slight that it is barely visible. This poses a problem for biohybrid robots designed to move using living muscles. Researchers at ETH Zurich have now demonstrated that it is not just the amount of muscle tissue that matters, but above all how the muscle and the artificial scaffold interact. Their bioactuators combine living skeletal muscle tissue, grown from mouse muscle cells, with a soft hydrogel scaffold. This soft, water-rich material bends and stretches like living tissue. What is new is that both parts are designed together as one system. The researchers first used a computer simulation to determine where and how much muscle tissue to place and what properties the hydrogel scaffold should have. Aiste Balciunaite and Mike Y. Michelis, co-lead authors of a study recently published in Nature Communications , jointly developed a new approach for this purpose. The muscle and the scaffold are designed together from the outset. Balciunaite, a doctoral student in the Soft Robotics Lab led by ETH Professor Robert Katzschmann, explains: “Instead of specifying a fixed form for our muscle geometry, we wanted to design the whole thing from scratch on the computer.” To do this, the researchers designed the muscle tissue configuration and the scaffold simultaneously on the computer, rather than one after the other. An algorithm searched for configurations in which the contraction of the muscle produced the greatest possible movement of the entire component. The researchers then built the computer-designed muscle actuators in the laboratory and tested them. The scaffolds were 3D-printed with light using a technique called xolography, which takes about one minute per scaffold. “Of course, it was an iterative process,” Balciunaite recalls. The experiments provided information on material properties and manufacturing conditions, which was fed back into the computer simulation. The result was the creation of what the researchers call bioactuators, each about 1.5 centimeters long. These actuators consist of living muscle tissue and an artificial hydrogel scaffold. They can flex so strongly that the movement is visible to the naked eye. The researchers report a range of motion up to eleven times greater than that of earlier systems with a comparable amount of muscle tissue. “With previous systems, you sometimes had to look under a microscope to see the flexing,” says Balciunaite. The newly developed bioactuators can jump, swim, move across a surface, and grasp objects. What impressed Balciunaite the most was the jumping. Jumping, she says, is an unusual movement that requires a particularly strong change in shape. For her, this experiment shows how important the interaction between the living muscle and the soft artificial scaffold is. With a single contraction, the actuator lifts itself about five millimeters off the bottom of the dish, a third of its body length. A walking version covers 6.2 millimeters per second, faster relative to its body length than any walking biohybrid robot reported so far. These small robots can move so powerfully not just because of their muscle tissue. It is crucial that the muscle and the scaffold form a seamless, firm connection. Fine grooves in the scaffold help the tissue anchor firmly and align its muscle fibers. This ensures that as little muscle strength as possible is lost during the transfer to the scaffold. For now, however, biohybrid robots depend on a nutrient solution that keeps their muscle tissue alive. Researchers are still a long way from developing a robot that can be used over the long term. Katzschmann explains that larger systems require an artificial blood supply: a vascular system that delivers oxygen and nutrients to the tissues and removes waste products. This is one of the biggest challenges for future development. Another challenge is the natural variability of living tissue. Unlike industrially manufactured components, cultured muscle actuators do not all behave exactly the same way. The researchers therefore aim to better understand and control how muscle tissue develops in the laboratory as it matures. For Katzschmann, the study shows above all the potential of the interaction between living tissue and soft artificial structures. Muscles can do more than generate force. They can change their shape, thereby influencing how a body moves and flexes. The muscle shape itself becomes something engineers can design, rather than a fixed constraint to work around. At the same time, the study shows how closely different fields of research need to work together to achieve this. Only through the interplay of cell biology, materials science, robotics, and computer-aided design was it possible to develop muscle tissue and an artificial scaffold as a single integrated system. For Katzschmann, this also offers longer-term potential: in the future, robotic systems could make greater use of the characteristics of living organisms, rather than relying solely on conventional motors and rigid components for movement. “We’re just beginning to build robots in a more natural way,” he says. Source: ETH Zurich The post Real muscles let tiny robots jump, swim, and grasp appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have developed an implantable system that clears excess glucose from the blood. Type 2 diabetes is becoming increasingly common worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, it is often linked to obesity, a sedentary lifestyle, and excess energy intake over many years. Although insulin injections can bring blood sugar levels down, they do not address the body’s chronic energy surplus. Insulin merely helps muscle cells take up glucose from the bloodstream, but if the body does not use that energy, the excess is converted into fat. This helps explain why many patients continue to gain weight despite treatment. Now, a team led by Martin Fussenegger has developed a potential new way to treat diabetes: an implantable system that uses an electrically powered catalyst to lower blood glucose. Fussenegger is a professor in ETH Zurich’s biosystems science and engineering department in Basel. The team’s findings appear in Science . For years, the Basel-based team of researchers has been exploring ways to tackle diabetes with systems that regulate blood sugar. Earlier approaches relied on specially developed genetic networks. However, these systems depend on biological components, which pose additional challenges in areas such as immune tolerance, stability, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. The new system gets around this problem with a catalyst made entirely from inorganic materials, which needs no cells, enzymes, or other biological components. It consists of graphite felt studded with gold nanoclusters, which are themselves decorated with even smaller platinum particles. The materials showed excellent biocompatibility in the experimental study, says Fussenegger. The team developed the catalyst’s nanostructured surface themselves. The implant also contains an electronic control unit housed in a 3D-printed casing. Power is supplied wirelessly at a frequency of 13.56 MHz, which is internationally designated for industrial, scientific and medical applications. The catalyst converts excess glucose in the blood into gluconate. This means that some of the glucose is no longer metabolized and stored in tissue, which also helps limit the build-up of body fat. The gluconate is then excreted in the urine. The catalyst is controlled wirelessly through a closed-loop system. A standard glucose sensor, like those commonly worn on the upper arm by people with diabetes, continuously monitors glucose levels in the tissue. If blood sugar rises too high after a meal, the sensor sends a signal via Bluetooth to a smartphone or smartwatch. The smart device then activates the catalyst, which uses electrical energy to convert the glucose. Once glucose levels have fallen to the desired level, the device switches itself off automatically, protecting patients from dangerously low blood sugar. In a laboratory experiment, Fussenegger’s team tested the system in a reservoir holding five liters of a glucose-containing nutrient solution—roughly the volume of blood in the human body. This showed that the catalyst was capable of converting glucose in this volume of solution. The researchers also tested the system in diabetic mice and found that the animals’ blood sugar could be precisely regulated. The mice lost weight, the implant was well tolerated, and it operated reliably during a six-week period. “The system operates at a very low voltage, and our experiments showed no evidence of tissue damage from either electrical or thermal effects,” says Fussenegger. The team has not yet tested the device on humans. Fussenegger sees the approach as a paradigm shift away from conventional drugs and towards scalable, electronically controlled treatments that can be integrated into digital environments such as the Internet of Things. “For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs,” he says. “And the catalyst only activates when glucose levels are too high.” The team now plans to develop the system into a medical device. Because the glucose-lowering mechanism itself works without cells or enzymes, technical development could be more straightforward. Another advantage is that the components needed to build such a device, including external control and wireless power transmission devices, have already been developed and are commercially available. Source: ETH Zurich The post Implant system could be a new way to treat type 2 diabetes appeared first on Futurity .
