items.descriptionOriginal: A new study finds celebrity digital twins may boost trust in customer service. Imagine losing your credit card, logging into your bank’s website for help, and being greeted by a virtual customer service representative who looks and sounds exactly like actor Hugh Jackman. The person helping you isn’t actually the Hollywood star—it’s his AI-powered digital twin. And the new research suggests that familiar face could significantly improve how you perceive your customer service experience. “When people see the familiar face of a famous person they like, there’s a halo effect,” says Lingyao (Ivy) Yuan, associate professor of information systems and business analytics in Iowa State University’s Ivy College of Business. “The positive feelings they have about that person can carry over to how they view the service, even before it begins.” In a study published in the Journal of Management Information Systems , Yuan and her coauthors examined a growing technology trend known as “Celebrity-as-a-Service,” an approach in which companies use AI-powered or human-operated digital replicas of celebrities to interact directly with customers. “We found customers may be more trusting of a service, more willing to use it and even more forgiving of mistakes when a virtual representative resembles a celebrity they already know and like,” Yuan says. Yuan says the study’s findings also offer a glimpse into a future where AI-powered “digital humans” become a routine part of everyday business. “We’re moving toward a world where interactions with digital humans will be increasingly common,” Yuan says. “The question isn’t just whether the technology works. It’s how people respond to it and how those responses shape the decisions they make.” Customers have long seen celebrities endorsing products in commercials and advertisements, but digital twins take that idea much further, Yuan says. “Instead of appearing in a one-way marketing campaign, a celebrity’s digital likeness can interact with customers in real time, answer their questions, solve problems, and complete transactions,” Yuan says. To examine how everyday customers react to digital twins, Yuan collaborated with fellow researchers Antino Kim, associate professor of information systems at Indiana University; Mike Seymour, a researcher in digital innovation at the University of Sydney; and Alan R. Dennis, a professor of information systems and chair of internet systems at Indiana University. The team’s question was simple: If two digital customer service representatives provide the same help, does it matter whether one looks like a celebrity? To find out, the researchers created a digital prototype, in compliance with US fair use law for research, using technology that placed actor Hugh Jackman’s face onto a digital representative. Yuan says Jackman was selected because he combined high name recognition with a largely positive public image, and his diverse career across film, television, and theater made him familiar to a wide range of participants. “This helped us isolate the effects of perceived celebrity status rather than familiarity with a specific type of performer,” Yuan says. The researchers conducted two controlled experiments in which participants interacted with either the celebrity version or a non-celebrity version of the representative, both of which provided the same assistance. Afterward, participants evaluated the experience across several measures, including whether the representative appeared “capable, benevolent and honest.” Yuan says the celebrity advantage was clear. “Participants consistently rated the digital celebrity agent more favorably across each of these measures, even though the quality of service never changed,” she says. The results highlighted a powerful psychological effect, Yuan says. Rather than judging the technology solely on its performance, “participants appeared to transfer some of their positive feelings about the celebrity to the service itself,” she says. “We know people often make quick judgments based on social cues, and a familiar, well-liked face can create positive expectations and boost trust.” The researchers also wanted to know what happens when technology makes mistakes. In a second experiment, Yuan and her team introduced common customer service errors, such as mishearing a name, misunderstanding an address or asking customers to repeat information. Typically, those mistakes erode trust and increase frustration, but participants interacting with the celebrity version were noticeably more forgiving and less quick to anger, Yuan says. “The positive feelings attached to the real-world celebrity acted as a psychological buffer against errors and softened customer judgment,” Yuan says. The researchers also didn’t find any evidence of “algorithm aversion,” Yuan adds, meaning participants weren’t more critical when a celebrity avatar was controlled by AI rather than by a human. The study’s findings could help companies design more effective digital customer service experiences, but Yuan says they also raise important questions for customers. As AI-powered “digital humans” become more common, companies may be able to customize virtual representatives for individual customers, “matching celebrities or digital assistants to a user’s specific age, language, or personal preferences.” Yuan says transparency and ethical guidelines will become increasingly important as the technology evolves, helping ensure customers always know when they are interacting with AI rather than an actual person. “Customers need to be aware that there is artificial intelligence behind it,” she says. “This technology has the potential to offer genuine value when used in a regulated and ethical way, and as our exposure to it grows, it’s important that we continue to build our shared awareness and understanding of it.” Yuan says the study also suggests that when it comes to AI, appearance matters. “A familiar face may not change how well a service works, but it can change how people feel about using it,” she says. Source: Iowa State University The post Celebrity faces may boost your trust in artificial intelligence appeared first on Futurity .

items.description: Περιγραφή επεισοδίου: Ένας έφηβος έχτισε ένα δίκτυο διανομής προμηθειών όπου οι οικογένειες ζητούν ό,τι χρειάζονται χωρίς να συμπληρώσουν καμία φόρμα ή να δηλώσουν ότι έχουν ανάγκη. items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: A teenager built a supply distribution network where families request what they need without filling out any forms or declaring themselves as someone in need. She also added a program that researches each family’s cultural background and sends handmade crafts alongside the package. That’s Vivian Ho, the first nominated Local Changemaker in The Optimist Daily’s new series. Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including six countries that just put a dollar figure on their EV investments, a Columbia University finding on the minimum movement needed to offset a desk job, and what pest experts actually recommend instead of vinegar. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Karissa: Hi, everyone. I’m Karissa. Arielle: I’m Arielle. Karissa: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. Arielle: So good to be back this week. It’s feeling very spooky over here. How about you, Karissa? Karissa: Super spooky and Halloweeny as we prepare for the holiday over the weekend, and a time change over in the US. I know over in Amsterdam, you’re already having those darker evenings. Arielle: Yes, we had our time change last weekend, and yeah, it does get dark so early, and it feels quite wintry, but that’s all right. Karissa: Mm-hmm. I miss the sun. I know. Maybe a week of this weather and I’ll be longing for the sun, but there is no shortage of good news to brighten your day at The Optimist Daily. Arielle: No, especially because we started publishing our Local Changemakers series this week on Wednesday. You can look forward to one Local Changemaker feature every Wednesday in the run-up to Thanksgiving. This week was a little bit different. We have two features because we have the Student Maker story, which kind of inspired us to highlight younger changemakers this year, and then the first nominated Local Changemaker. Karissa: Mm-hmm. I can’t wait to dive into them. But before we do- Mm … that, we wanna remind you that all these solutions are available in our newsletter format, whether you want that every day or just a weekly digest. It’s free to sign up, and the link to do that is in the show notes. Arielle: If you’re more of a social media feed type of news consumer, then you can follow us on all social platforms, @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are, @OdeToOptimism. You can also reach me and Karissa directly by emailing us at podcast@optimistdaily.com. We really love getting comments, questions, feedback, or anecdotes that you wanna share with us. So yeah, feel free to shoot us an email whenever. Karissa: We also encourage you to share with friends, loved ones, all this positive news from The Optimist Daily, and remind them that, you know, good things are happening out there in the world. As usual, a big thank you to our Emissaries who financially support the mission of The Optimist Daily. If you would like to become an Emissary, the link to do that is also in the show notes. With all of that said and done, shall we jump into the spooky solutions of the week? Let’s get into it. Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician Karissa: The first solution is “Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician”. This piece is informed by an actual pediatrician about how to make Halloween work for every kid in your family, and the framing is really specific to each age group in a way that’s genuinely useful. For toddlers, one tip that I thought stood out was to bring a wagon, even if your kid insists they don’t need one when you’re trick-or-treating or attending some kind of Halloween event. For school-aged kids, uh, Dr. Kristen Cook, who is the pediatrician that gives all this advice in the article, frames Halloween as giving earned independence when you’re trick-or-treating, so you can, you know, hang back a couple houses, let the kids lead, but keep them in sight. And then when it comes to teenagers, they might be going to Halloween parties, and at these parties they can come across some peer pressuring situations. It’s good to talk to them about an exit plan for situations they might not be comfortable with and discuss how to deal with these potentially uncomfortable situations, but ultimately trusting them to handle it the right way. So lots of good tips here. This just brings so much Halloween nostalgia back for me. Arielle: Yeah, I, um… my parents didn’t let me participate in Halloween growing up. I know. Heartbreak. I think it just was, uh, you know, we are an immigrant family coming from a very Christian country- Yes, yeah … and they kind of saw it as, like, kind of like devil worship. But, you know, we got over that stage. I was already, um… I kinda aged out of Halloween, uh, in the traditional sense where you go trick-or-treating and all of that. But my youngest sister was able to participate, and she had, like, really fun costumes. As a little kid, she wanted to be a tissue box one year. Um- That’s a good one … which was really weird. It was, like, a High School Musical tissue box, because we had like, High School Musical, um, wrapping paper. And so that’s how she decided to dress up. Karissa: I love it. Arielle: Yeah, so I have vicarious Halloween memories through my youngest sister. Karissa: Well, I mean, as an adult now, maybe you can do some, some of this stuff. NYC food pantries are stocking pet food for struggling households Karissa: The next solution is very heartwarming, and it’s that “New York City food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households”. New York State just put $500,000 towards making sure pet owners don’t have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their animals. There are now 22 food pantries across all five boroughs stocking free pet food, and the reason this program exists is kind of heartbreaking and kind of sweet at the same time. The story mentions a woman named Cassandra in Brooklyn who sometimes eats less so her Shih Tzu doesn’t go hungry, and she’s far from alone. The demand for pet food grew after SNAP benefit cuts, which tells you a lot about just how far those cuts reach into people’s lives. Animal welfare groups have known for years that financial hardship and pet surrender are directly linked, but this program is essentially trying to catch families before they hit that wall. 5 research-backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk Karissa: The next solution is a health lifestyle related one, and it’s “Five research backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk”. Columbia University researchers ran a study trying to find the minimum effective dose of movement to counteract sitting all day. The answer was actually surprisingly specific. It’s simply five minutes of walking every 30 minutes that makes a difference. NPR actually then tested that with 20,000 of their listeners and found the exact same thing. So this article breaks down that finding plus four other fixes. Arielle, have you ever heard of this tip to walk five minutes every 30 minutes? Arielle: No, but to increase focus, I use the Pomodoro Technique, which is when you set the timer for about 20- 25 minutes and then give yourself a five-minute break. Because I work from home- Yeah … I am always kind of hunched over my laptop. So that is a trick that I use, and I do generally get up and, like, walk around the house. Um- Yeah … so I guess my body intuitively knew that this was a good thing to do, but it’s nice to have the science back it up. Karissa: The whole concept of this kind of, like, movement snack, um, short burst of activity is catching fire and a good suggestion. I guess I’ll mention one more thing about this solution, but you can check out the rest on optimistdaily.com. The whole posture section of this article talks about how the idea of sitting up straight and holding it advice is actually not correct. The actual physical therapist guidance is that your best posture is your next posture, meaning any fixed position causes strain eventually. New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries Karissa: Well, the next solution is “New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries”. NJ Transit has been installing art exhibitions at train and bus stations since 2019, and the program just expanded to its eighth location. The new show is about railroads and 250 years of American history, which is a pretty fun yet informative thing to encounter while you’re just trying to catch your train, the history about railroads. But the whole premise of this is that transit spaces are great for public art because nobody goes there expecting to see any. The encounter is accidental, which makes it different from an intentional gallery visit. I really like this, um, rise of art in public spaces, and it kind of reminds me of a solution we shared a couple months ago about how over in Warsaw they’re putting libraries in commuter stations. So if you have a little time, a layover in transportation, you can go check out the library. So I think this is a really cool kind of global trend. Arielle: And it’s really nice that the program actually pays the artists stipends because public art rarely comes with a real budget, and a lot of the time public art is like a, a mural that maybe someone painted for free or graffiti, which honestly, I’m a huge fan of graffiti. Some of the tags are really impressive, and some of them- Yeah … are just kind of silly, but they’re entertaining in their own way. Um, but that obviously doesn’t come with payment. If anything, it might come with a fine. Karissa: Right. Exactly. In this broader conversation about what public spaces are for, whether that’s a transit station, a library, park, you know, it can be a lot more than just something that people move through. Student Makers: bringing free STEM to students on three continents Karissa: Moving on to the Changemaker series, we talked more about Student Makers in this deeper dive. They are a group bringing free STEM to students on three continents. And like Arielle mentioned, this is the story that made us decide to make the entire series this year about people under 30, because young people are really just doing so many impressive things to change the world. At Student Makers, former students become the instructors. It’s often high schoolers teaching middle schoolers, and the founder’s whole argument is that it’s more relatable to have, um, you know, people who are closer in age to you to help teach things than an adult expert teaching the same material. Like we mentioned, we’ll have some of the main players behind Student Makers on the podcast in the beginning of 2027, which is crazy to even say that 2027 is around the corner. But we look forward to welcoming them on and hearing directly from them. Meet Vivian Ho: the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity Arielle: I will take over from here, Karissa, and my first solution is actually the first nominated changemaker for this series. The title- Ooh … of the article is “Meet Vivian Ho, the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity”. Most programs that distribute supplies to low-income families ask that family to identify themselves before they get anything. So basically, you have to fill out a form, you check a box, you explain your situation to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built her nonprofit, All the Same organization, around removing that whole process. Families request what they need anonymously, and nobody has to declare themselves as someone in need to get the help they need. And she started this at just 16, which is quite impressive. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: The anonymous sign-up system is what makes this really special. Vivian’s read on situations like this was that the stigma of asking for help was keeping families from asking at all. So she just said, “Let’s get rid of that.” There’s also something within this nonprofit. There’s another, uh, initiative called the Cultural Surprises program, and it’s something I hadn’t seen before. So volunteers research the cultural background of the family they’re packing for, and handmade crafts reflecting that culture go out alongside the supply package, and it turns a resource delivery into something more like recognition, something that makes that family feel really seen. I’m not gonna get into all of the details, but I do encourage people who are interested in learning more about Vivian Ho and perhaps how to support her work to check out the article because it is really, really remarkable that she was able to do this as a teenager. Karissa: Congratulations to Vivian for being nominated by two of The Optimist Daily community members who are involved with the project as well, a nomination from her co-founder and a volunteer that she inspired to start his own project nominated Vivian. So go check that out if you wanna learn more. Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems Arielle: The next solution is titled “Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems”. Kenya just signed a $160 million deal to protect nearly 67,000 square miles of some of the most important wildlife habitat in Africa, including the Maasai Mara and Tsavo. But the interesting part isn’t just the money, it’s the structure of how that money gets released, because this isn’t a grant that arrives and then disappears. So the funding mechanism is called Project Finance for Permanence. Money flows in tied to specific government policy benchmarks, and not all the money gets, uh, given upfront, let’s say. If Kenya doesn’t hit the milestones, then those funds never get released. Tsavo holds 40% of Kenya’s elephants and 20% of its critically endangered black rhinos, and that’s just to give you an idea of what’s at stake for wildlife and geographically. Kenya committed to the global 30 by 30 target and was sitting at about 20% to 23% coverage, so this deal would largely close that gap by 2030. Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works Arielle: The next solution is titled, “Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works.” So every fall, people reach for the vinegar bottle as a first line of pest defense. They spray the windows, they spray the door frames, and then it feels like they’ve done something. But two pest control experts basically say, “You’ve done nothing.” The reason why is in this article, and there’s also one fall tip in here that’s actually kind of strange and useful. So vinegar unfortunately only kills soft-bodied insects on direct wet contact, and then once it dries, then the vinegar doesn’t really do anything against cockroaches, beetles, spiders, or ants. And researchers found negligible effects on most common household insects. What really works is, like, caulking windows and weather-stripping doors and adding door sweeps. That will actually stop bugs from getting in. Spraying is just treating the symptom and not really addressing the entry point of where all of these pests try to come in and get cozy ’cause the weather outside is getting worse. Um- Yeah … and then the, the weird tip, well, I found it weird or unexpected, is the acorn tip. If you are bringing acorns or pine cones inside this fall, then you should put them in 150-degree Fahrenheit oven for about 30 minutes first, and that will kill whatever’s living inside them, and then you can, like, decorate your home for the holidays in peace knowing that there’s no hidden critter in your pine cone just waiting to make your house their home. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: The DIY home pest control has surged since the pandemic. People want low-chemical solutions, and that’s why I think vinegar gets so much reach. But yeah, unfortunately it’s just not as effective as everyone thought it was. Karissa: Well, it’s good to know so we don’t waste our vinegar and our time. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Yeah. Karissa: I- I have to say, though, maybe this is bad, but I do like to use just the harsh chemicals and get them out of the way- … if they do come in the house. So I, I don’t hesitate to use the big stuff. Arielle: Yeah. It’s… You know, we appreciate your honesty here. I’m sure there are a lot of listeners who struggle with pests and are like, “Yeah, I’m just gonna obliterate.” The 7 best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs Arielle: The next solution is titled, “The seven best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs”. Grocery prices are unfortunately still high, and two university horticulture experts say there are specific vegetables that genuinely pay for themselves when you grow them at home. Most of the list made sense to me, but there’s one of them that takes three years before it really starts producing, and both experts say plant it anyway. And yeah, there are pretty good reasons, which I will get into. So first, herbs are the economic winner here. They’re among the most expensive produce per ounce at the grocery store. You usually buy more than you use, and growing them means you harvest exactly what you need when you need it. The strange one was the asparagus. It takes two to three years of establishment before you get a real harvest, so you really have to be committed to the asparagus, and also you have to like asparagus. I like asparagus, but I know a lot of people aren’t the biggest fans. But a well-maintained bed produces for up to 20 years. One expert calls it something you’ll have basically for life. Both experts are clear that the garden only saves money if you plant what your household actually eats. So start with vegetables you already go through the most, and that will help you save money in the end. How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility Arielle: The last solution that we are gonna share with everyone this week is titled “How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility”. So there is that conflict in Iran that has been driving oil prices up 33% this year. But six European countries collectively avoided nearly $2.2 billion in oil import costs just because they have enough EVs on the road. That’s not a projection or a goal, that’s an actual number from a six-month window. Denmark alone displaced 13% of its entire 2025 oil consumption. So there’s a real dollar security argument for EV adoption here that goes beyond anything to do with the environment, although the environment is very important. Karissa: Yes. Arielle: Hopefully this, uh, this will encourage other economies to really invest in their EV development, but also hopefully this conflict ends soon. Karissa: Yeah. So- For multiple reasons, of course. But it just goes to show how moving towards renewable energy, sustainable energy across the board is just the best path towards energy security. Arielle: Definitely. Well, those were all of the solutions we had this week, but before we go, we have a positive quote. Karissa: This week we have, “Part of being optimistic is keeping one’s head pointed toward the sun, one’s feet moving forward.” And that’s from Nelson Mandela. Arielle: Beautiful. Well, everyone, I hope you enjoy your Halloween weekend if you’re celebrating, and if not, then I hope you enjoy the, uh, candy sales that are inevitably- going to happen after Halloween is over. We will both be back next week with more solutions. Karissa: Until then, have a great weekend. The post Podcast Transcript October 30th, 2026— Kenya’s wildlife deal, Halloween tips across the ages, and EV energy security first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.titleOriginal: From Bipolar Diagnosis To Bestselling Author — ‘I Do Not Consider Myself Unwell’
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο δημοσιεύτηκε σε συνεργασία με την India Mental Health Alliance. Η Aparna Piramal Raje είναι συγγραφέας, αρθρογράφος, συγγραφέας μπεστ σέλερ και μητέρα δύο παιδιών. Έχει επίσης ζήσει με διπολική διαταραχή για πάνω από δύο δεκαετίες. Εδώ, μοιράζεται τις επτά «θεραπείες» - από την αγάπη της οικογένειάς της μέχρι μια ρουτίνα ύπνου που αποκαλεί «θρησκεία» - που τη βοηθούν…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article has been published in partnership with India Mental Health Alliance. Aparna Piramal Raje is a writer, columnist, bestselling author, and mother of two. She has also lived with bipolar disorder for over two decades. Here, she shares the seven 'therapies' — from her family's love to a sleep routine she calls 'religion' — that help her live a full, happy life. It is March 2013, and I am at a yoga ashram in Bihar for a weeklong retreat. And I am coming apart. I haven't slept more than three hours a night in several days. I'm talking to myself. There are voices in my head, and my thoughts are so scattered and disorganised that I can't hold on to any of them. I am having a psychotic breakdown. When the retreat ends, I can't manage the journey back to Mumbai on my own. My husband has to come and get me, and escort me home. Aparna beside a poster for a 2022 talk about her book and her mental health journey. Seeing the state I'm in, I'm taken to a psychiatrist and put on medication. And for the first time, what I have been living with gets a name: bipolar disorder, a serious mental health condition. Thirteen years without a name The diagnosis was new. The condition was not. It had first surfaced in the year 2000, when I was in my mid-20s, and remained undiagnosed for more than a decade. I had been raised in Mumbai and London and studied at Harvard Business School and Oxford University. I had worked in my family's office furniture business and as a journalist. Through all of it, I had been riding highs and lows I didn't understand. Aparna pictured horse riding with her sister, who remains one of her closest sources of support. Looking back, I can see the pattern. Too many projects and deadlines pushed me into mania more than once, in both jobs. Work, for me, had become a trigger. After the ashram, I recovered from the psychosis, only to be plunged into depression for several months. Eventually, I came out of that too. " I don't consider myself unwell, even though it is an illness" It may sound strange, but the diagnosis came as a relief. For the first time, my family and I had a roadmap for how to treat and manage what was happening to me. Aparna began studying at Harvard Business School in 2000, the year her symptoms first surfaced. It also taught me what bipolar disorder actually is. As I understand it, it is a mood disorder brought on by psychological triggers and chemical imbalances in the brain. It causes extreme shifts in mood. At one end is mania: energetic phases where I barely sleep, have delusions of grandeur, and sometimes tip into psychosis. At the other end is depression, when I am low on energy and in low spirits. In between, there are long stretches of stability and normalcy, though every patient's cycles are different. Aparna with her sister Radhika in their 20s; she later described her sister as a key support. Everyone has mood swings, so please don't assume you are bipolar because you have some. Bipolar disorder means extreme swings, and very specific changes in behaviour. Most importantly, the diagnosis showed me that personality and illness are different things. I have a normal personality. I also have a medical condition that needs to be managed and treated, like any other medical condition. Aparna photographed in Laax in March 2018, during a manic episode, five years after her bipolar disorder diagnosis. So I don't consider myself unwell, even though it is an illness. That insight became the bedrock of my self-acceptance — and without self-acceptance, no healing can take place. Learning to survive I'm an optimist by nature, and I always look for solutions. Over the next ten years, it was these solutions and "hacks" that helped me heal and recover. It took a lot to make everything come together: the right medication, a trustworthy doctor, supportive family and friends, a manageable job, a spiritual practice, self-reflection, and fulfilling lifestyle pursuits. At times, it felt like a matter of tremendous planetary alignment! Aparna at the 2015 launch of Working Out of the Box, which preceded Chemical Khichdi. But I came to see that three "therapies" are essential just to survive, especially in a crisis. None of them can be substituted. The first is medical therapy. I see my psychiatrist, take additional medication when I need it, and continue talk therapy. I cannot stress enough how much a good therapist matters. As I understand it, my mood episodes are psychological triggers causing chemical imbalances. If I haven't slept well for five nights in a row, I'm likely to tip into hypomania. But what is keeping me awake for five nights in a row? That is usually something psychological. Aparna with her husband Amit, whom she credits as a key part of her support system. Therapy helps me find those triggers, understand myself, and manage my mood swings. I've seen therapists for two decades, and they've given me incredible insight into what lies beneath my ups and downs. I still see mine every fortnight. It is essential to my stability. The second is love therapy — the care of the people closest to me. For me, that is my husband, my two sons and my sister. All of them look after me when I'm unwell, and I'm lucky to have their unconditional support and acceptance. Aparna with relatives at a family gathering; she says family support is central to her recovery. The third is lifestyle therapy. Self-care turned out to be just as necessary as doctors and caregivers. A disciplined lifestyle matters for everyone, but especially for those of us living with a mental health challenge. I exercise regularly, play games, and eat a nutritious diet. But sleep, as far as I'm concerned, is religion. A regular sleep routine is the single biggest factor in my emotional and mental well-being, and I'm much happier now that I'm disciplined about it. Aparna with friends; she describes trusted relationships as important to managing her health. So I have dinner at home with my husband and kids most evenings. I rarely go out at night more than twice a week, and I don't work after dinner. Most nights, I get my seven to eight hours. Learning to thrive Surviving is one thing. Thriving — being well enough to write a book, or to stand before strangers and talk about my mental health — needed something more. It needed self-reflection, self-inquiry and inner work. That is where the other four therapies came in. Self-therapy began on the page. I journal, I use positive affirmations, and I keep returning to both to understand what triggers my mood swings and how to regulate my emotions. Aparna visited her Oxford college in 2025; she studied at Oxford before her 2013 diagnosis. Spiritual therapy came through a regular study of Vedanta. It helped me look at the root causes of my ups and downs, and it has made me calmer and more at peace. The therapy of empathy came from other people. Mental health, I've learnt, is a team sport, so I made a point of asking for help. I shared my vulnerability with many friends, mentors and colleagues, and it made a huge difference. Aparna at a panel discussion for Working Out of the Box, published before Chemical Khichdi. These allies made safe spaces for me to share my thoughts and emotions, during manic or depressive phases and in recovery afterwards. They turned listening into an art form. They offered acceptance, patience, empathy and advice without judgement — and sometimes stepped in directly when things got difficult. If it takes a village to raise a child, it takes a community of allies to heal a mind. Aparna's book 'Chemical Khichdi' chronicles her journey of living with bipolar disorder and recovery. Work therapy was the one I least expected. Work had pushed me into mania before, so how could it ever be therapeutic? Over time, I learnt that structured, fulfilling work could be an anchor. Approached with the right balance and intention, it gives me stability and meaning, along with a sense of control, accomplishment and identity. It is no longer only about income or career. It is a way to channel my energy constructively, and to build the routines that help me manage my moods. Aparna at an event marking her first independent board appointment during her working life. The strategy that makes this possible is what I call playing 'opposite-handed'. Imagine playing a sport with your other hand: you'd play more mindfully and more slowly. That's how I now work. I recognise my limits and take breaks before I burn out, and this has let me thrive at work despite how unpredictable bipolar disorder can be. Aparna teaching a group of students; she describes fulfilling work as a source of stability. Together, these four therapies helped me understand myself, regulate myself, and move from just coping to thriving. Back on the stage By May 2022, I had been stable for over four years. That month, I stood on stage at the Royal Opera House in Mumbai, one of India's most prestigious theatres, in front of 400 people. I made a speech, and my sister and I released my book, Chemical Khichdi: How I Hacked My Mental Health — the story of my journey of healing and recovery. Aparna at the launch of Chemical Khichdi, her 2022 book about her mental health journey. It went on to become an official national bestseller. Over the next few years, I was invited to speak at 150 talks across the country and online, breaking taboos about mental health. Then, in November 2025, I stood on a stage in Bangalore among eleven brave women, each of us holding a copy of Homecoming: Mental Health Journeys of Resilience, Healing and Wholeness. Written by Neha Kirpal and Dr Nandini Murali, it is a unique anthology of Indian women's mental health journeys, and mine is one of them. Aparna with other women at a 2025 event for Homecoming, an anthology of mental health journeys. A few years earlier, Neha and I had talked about her hopes of writing a book. Now Chemical Khichdi was being seen as a forerunner in a growing movement of mental health books in India, and I was beginning to be seen as a mental health advocate. It was deeply satisfying. Happy, thriving and bipolar Today, I'm 50. I live in Mumbai with my husband, our two teenage sons and my in-laws, and I work as a writer, columnist and public speaker. In more than two decades of living with bipolar disorder, I've had about a dozen episodes of mania, or its milder form, hypomania. That's quite a lot. But I haven't had a full-blown manic episode or depression in over eight years, and I have a "normal" personal and professional life. Aparna at a Chemical Khichdi launch event; the book later became a national bestseller. The mood swings haven't vanished. I still feel things with more intensity and volatility than most people. The difference is that I'm in control now (well, most of the time). I've learnt to witness my emotions without being consumed by them, using these seven therapies. I believe happiness is a decision. For me, it is a choice and a daily practice, and these therapies are my everyday toolkit. Aparna signing copies of Chemical Khichdi, which led to invitations to speak across India. I have also come to realise that my vulnerability is my guru. My bipolarity has been my biggest source of illumination. Nearly ten years ago, I wrote this in my journal: "I have come to realise that the stronger you are, the more hurt you can handle. And the less you share that hurt with anyone, the more the accumulated emotion. I've experienced every possible negative emotion - anger, frustration, resentment, fear and paranoia. It has made me volatile, manic, uncontrollable, deluded, sleep-deprived and generally a pain to handle. Aparna at a book club gathering; she continues to work as a writer, columnist and speaker. But from that has emerged so much that's good about my life: truth, compassion, wisdom, patience and most of all, love. Could I live without being bipolar? Absolutely. And my family would echo that ten times over. But it has provided me the opportunity to examine my life like no other." If you're where I once was I've come a long way since that ashram in 2013. So here is what I'd want you to know. There's no need to be scared of a mental health condition. In my experience, it can be managed like any physical health condition. Recognise the symptoms early, and respond before things escalate. It's difficult at first, but it gets much easier with time, and it doesn't have to stand in the way of a family life, a social life or a career. Aparna speaking about Chemical Khichdi; she has delivered talks on mental health across India. Take charge of your mental health. Get timely professional advice. Tell your family what's going on, and accept their help. Rest and slow down when you need to. Make allies, and open up to them. And develop your own therapies and hacks. Whether you live with bipolar disorder or any other mental health condition, I hope my story encourages you to get help when you need it. You can live the life you want to.

items.descriptionOriginal: After sugarcane is crushed for its juice, a fibrous residue called bagasse is left behind. At sugar mills, heaps of this material can be seen awaiting their next use. While some bagasse is already used to generate energy or make paper, it also holds potential for products that can replace plastic — and even become a source of protein. Across India, entrepreneurs and young innovators are exploring these possibilities. From compostable plates and takeaway boxes to fermentation-based protein, here are four ventures finding new value in sugarcane waste. 1. Chuk: Turning sugarcane fibre into compostable tableware When Ved Krishna returned to his family's paper business in Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, he began questioning the environmental cost of conventional food packaging. Plastic-coated and laminated materials were widely used, yet their disposal posed a growing problem. In 2017, his family's company, Pakka Limited, launched Chuk to offer an alternative. The brand uses bagasse, the fibrous residue left after sugarcane juice extraction, to manufacture plates, bowls, food containers and other tableware. The fibre is processed into pulp, which is then moulded into finished products. The resulting tableware is designed to be sturdy enough for everyday food service while offering an alternative to conventional plastic and Styrofoam disposables. Ved Krishna's Chuk uses sugarcane bagasse to make compostable plates, bowls and food containers for everyday food service. Photograph: ( TRASH ) Chuk's products are used by food and hospitality businesses, including Haldiram's, Starbucks and Chai Point. According to the company's earlier reporting, its tableware can decompose within approximately 60 days under suitable conditions. By giving sugarcane residue a second life, Chuk demonstrates how an agricultural byproduct can become a practical replacement for disposable plastic products. 3. Ecoware: Packaging that can return to the soil After witnessing the scale of plastic pollution in India, Rhea Mazumdar Singhal left her pharmaceutical career in the UK to work on an alternative to single-use packaging. She founded Ecoware in 2010, building a business around plant-based food-service products. Sugarcane bagasse is among the principal materials used in its range of plates, bowls, trays and takeaway containers. The fibre is converted into pulp and shaped under high heat and pressure using precision moulds. Ecoware says its products contain no plastic lining, adhesive, laminate or coating, allowing the material to break down naturally under suitable conditions. Founded by Rhea Mazumdar Singhal, Ecoware turns plant-based materials, including sugarcane fibre, into alternatives to single-use plastic packaging. Photograph: ( Lifestyle Asia ) The company reports that its products can biodegrade in soil in around 100 days in the presence of microbes. Its range is designed for practical food-service needs, including serving hot meals and packing takeaway orders. Ecoware's approach addresses two problems at once : the accumulation of disposable plastic and the underuse of agricultural residue. By offering businesses and households a plant-based alternative, it helps make lower-waste food packaging a more accessible everyday choice. 3. Dinearth: Making sustainable food packaging more accessible Dinearth, a sustainable packaging initiative founded by Harsh and Jani, backed by Abhinav Industries, brings bagasse-based alternatives to the food-service sector. The business draws on its parent company's experience in food packaging to offer products designed for restaurants, takeaway counters and catering businesses. Its manufacturing process begins with sugarcane bagasse sourced from sugar mills. The residue is converted into pulp and pressed into moulds using heat and pressure to create disposable food packaging. Its catalogue includes plates, trays, bowls and takeaway boxes, offering businesses alternatives to plastic and Styrofoam containers. Dinearth's EcoDine range offers bagasse-based plates, bowls and takeaway boxes, with select products reportedly priced from around Re 1 per unit. Photograph: ( Otarapack ) An important part of this approach is making the switch practical for smaller food vendors, not just large restaurant chains. Dinearth's EcoDine range has been presented as a more affordable line of biodegradable tableware, with reported prices starting at around Rs1 per unit for select products. By combining familiar food-service formats with plant-fibre materials, Dinearth seeks to make alternatives to conventional disposables easier to adopt across a wider range of businesses. 4. Kinva Bio: Exploring sugarcane waste as a source of protein What if agricultural residue could help meet the demand for protein? That is the question behind Kinva Bio, a venture developed by students Nitish and Gulshan Kumar at the National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management in Haryana. Instead of turning bagasse into a disposable product, the team is exploring how fungal fermentation can convert agricultural byproducts into mycoprotein, a protein-rich material produced using fungi. Sugarcane bagasse serves as one of the potential feedstocks. By giving agricultural residue a new purpose, Indian innovators are exploring alternatives to plastic disposables and new uses for biomass. Photograph: (AI generated using reference) The process combines biotechnology with artificial intelligence. Fungal fermentation converts the biomass, while an AI-powered digital twin helps predict protein yields and optimise production conditions. The aim is to develop a way of producing protein that could require less land and water than conventional sources. Kinva Bio remains an emerging innovation rather than an established, large-scale food producer. Its work nevertheless points to another possibility for agricultural waste: using biotechnology to turn low-value residue into a potential food resource. Sources: 'Ayodhya-based CHUK is turning sugarcane waste into sustainable cutlery for Indian Railways, Google, Amazon' by Rashi Varshney for YourStory, Published on 30 December 2020. Οι ερευνητές διαπίστωσαν ότι το 54% των συμμετεχόντων κάτω των 45 ετών που ακολούθησαν εντατική δίαιτα και πρόγραμμα άσκησης πέτυχαν ύφεση, σε σύγκριση με μόλις 4…
items.descriptionOriginal: A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care.

items.descriptionOriginal: Food accounts for a third of humanity’s greenhouse emissions. And sure enough, the most carbon-gushing foods are also the ones that tend to be the worst for our health, such as meats and dairy. So what if we tried taxing that carbon, to nudge people toward higher-plant diets that are healthier for people and planet alike? A new study in Nature Food explores how these food emissions taxes could be applied to countries around the world with different levels of wealth and greenhouse emissions. It shows how they could be tweaked to manage the delicate interplay between food prices, poverty, hunger, and health—while still cutting billions of tons of annual emissions. Economists have estimated that growing populations and increasing meat consumption worldwide could cause the environmental footprint of our food—including greenhouse emissions— to balloon by 50 to 90 percent by 2050 . This has spurred recommendations that humanity shift its diet , toward fewer animals and more plants. Emissions taxes paid by consumers buying foods are one way to encourage a shift away from meats, dairy, eggs , and sugars . But questions remain about how those taxes can be applied fairly to countries around the world—given that wealthier nations have more ability to pay them, and that many of these same nations also contributed disproportionately to rising greenhouse gases in the first place. In the new study, researchers used economic, trade, and public health models to predict how well different types of taxes would curb greenhouse emissions—and also, how they would impact food prices They compared two tax scenarios. In one, emissions are priced the same worldwide, at a constant cost of USD$ 185 per metric ton of CO 2 equivalent (tCO 2 eq). In this system, wealthy countries would still pay more taxes, because their food systems emit more tons of CO 2 . In the other system, the cost-per-ton of emissions is scaled up or down, based on each country’s wealth—thereby further increasing the taxes paid by consumers in wealthy countries (to as much as $969 per tCO 2 eq), while reducing those paid by lower-wealth countries (to as little as $21 per tCO 2 eq). The researchers compared these two scenarios both with and without a second provision, in which governments would also subsidize fruits and vegetables to further lower the prices that consumers pay for these low-carbon foods. Their results suggest that taxes based on a fixed-price-per-ton would reduce food-related emissions most sharply—by up to 18.7 percent, or about 2.6 billion tCO 2 eq worldwide each year. But such taxes would likely worsen overall health in some countries such as India, Bangladesh, and Vietnam—even after accounting for reductions in heart disease and diabetes—because they might make food less affordable to some people, compromising nutrition. The authors found that adjusting the price-per-ton of emissions based on national wealth would lessen this problem. And subsidizing the cost of fruits and vegetables would further decrease it. Together these two tweaks slightly reduced the emissions that were prevented—but they were still predicted to cut worldwide food emissions by 17 percent, or about 2.3 billion tCO 2 eq per year. The authors recommended that these efforts to reduce the negative impacts on the poor could be further explored, with detailed studies of poverty in individual countries, and potentially by excluding some critical sustenance foods such as fish or rice from the taxes in some countries. Bouyssou, et al. “ Food emissions taxes can deliver health and environmental benefits with limited leakage .” Nature Food , 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine

items.titleOriginal: Once Artists, Now Teachers Too: This Delhi Diwali Mela Will Put Neurodivergent Children in the Lead
items.description: Στην καρδιά του Νότιου Δελχί, σε ένα γραφικό πάρκο, καθώς ο ήλιος αρχίζει να δύει και το αεράκι του χειμώνα δύει σταδιακά, τρεις νέοι νευροαποκλίνοντες καλλιτέχνες, ηλικίας 14 και 17 ετών, θα εγκατασταθούν με τους καμβάδες και τις ζωγραφιές τους. Οι μαθητές τους; Περισσότερα από 50 άτομα που έχουν εγγραφεί για να μάθουν αφηρημένη τέχνη από αυτούς. Για αυτούς τους νέους καλλιτέχνες, το Diwali Art Mela είναι…
items.descriptionOriginal: At the heart of South Delhi, in a quaint park, as the sun begins to set and the winter breeze gradually sets in, three young neurodivergent artists, aged 14 and 17, will settle down with their canvases and paints. Their students? More than 50 people who have signed up to learn abstract art from them. For these young artists, the Diwali Art Mela is more than an opportunity to exhibit and sell their paintings. It is a chance to take on a different role — that of teachers and mentors — and have people recognise their abilities, creativity and leadership. The idea is central to what Rashmi Aggarwal, founder of Arts and Dreams, hopes to achieve through the initiative. She wants people to look beyond the neurodivergence of these children and see them for their artistic abilities. For Rashmi, the journey began at home. Her younger son, Pranav, who is now 14, started creating art when he was six. His paintings became a way for him to express his feeling s and offer his family a glimpse into his world. "We kept thinking about how to put artists in a place where people see their talent and not that they are neurodivergent. This can happen when they train others," she says. The first edition of the Diwali Art Mela is being organised by Arts and Dreams in collaboration with Children in India and Cure India Foundation. It will bring together art, creativity and inclusion. Visitors can explore paintings and artwork-based products such as calendars and wall hangings, participate in games and workshops, and interact with the artists. The event will also feature neurodivergent children making chocolates. When a mother's concern became a larger mission For Rashmi, the journey began at home. Her younger son, Pranav, who is now 14, started creating art when he was six. His paintings became a way for him to express his feeling s and offer his family a glimpse into his world. "His paintings always gave us a view of his world. He was creating a world of his own through colours. As a mother, I wanted him to get recognised for his art," she says. But Rashmi soon began thinking about other neurodivergent children who had artistic talent but limited access to the art world. She wanted to build something that would benefit not just Pranav, but other young artists like him. In 2024, Rashmi and her elder son, Lakshya Aggarwal, founded Arts and Dreams with this vision. What began as an effort to provide artists with a platform to exhibit and sell their paintings gradually expanded into creating art-based products that could help them earn from their work. Today, the initiative has 55 artists on board. When a product featuring an artist's work is sold, 20 per cent of the profit is shared with the artist as royalty. So far, 20 artists have received a cumulative Rs 4 lakh in royalties. One moment that reinforced the initiative's potential came when Arts and Dreams received a corporate order from a Japanese customer for 10,000 calendars. For Rashmi, however, the impact goes beyond the money. "They may not understand money as a concept, but they understand appreciation. They are on top of the world when they know someone liked their work and is taking it home," she says. One moment that reinforced the initiative's potential came when Arts and Dreams received a corporate order from a Japanese customer for 10,000 calendars. Featuring 13 artworks alongside photographs of the artists, the calendars travelled to people who may not otherwise have encountered their work or known about neurodivergent artists. "The story of the kids is travelling with the art," Rashmi says. The artists taking the lead At the Diwali Art Mela, Pranav will be among the three young artists conducting workshops for visitors. For Pranav, the workshop will focus on abstract bloom painting, using colours such as pink, green and yellow. He enjoys painting and hopes to explore feather painting next. When asked how he feels when someone buys his artwork, his answer is simple: " Achha lagta hai (it feels nice). I will proudly tell my friends about it too." That sense of appreciation is precisely what Rashmi hopes more people will experience — both as buyers of the artwork and as participants in the workshops. Aishwarya hopes to teach people how to paint nature on canvas. Aishwarya, who is 17 years old, will also sit alongside Pranav to teach participants. This time, she hopes to teach people how to paint nature on canvas. "For this mela, I plan to use acrylic paints with red, blue, and yellow as the main colors." We asked her what Diwali means to her, and she says with joy, "It's a festival I love. Everything about Diwali – the pretty lights, new clothes, crackers, sweets – makes me happy." She proudly shares that around 500 of her artworks have been sold so far, and she is always motivated to continue painting. The third mentor is Aarush, a 14-year-old, bold and confident boy. Aarush has been painting since he was three. Drawn to nature and wildlife, he often finds inspiration in what he observes around him. At the mela, he will be teaching participants how to draw and paint a boat using blue and white acrylic paints. "I was inspired by this sight in Nainital," he shares. He works with watercolours and structural painting, and his artwork has always received a good response at exhibitions. His mother says Aarush enjoys drawing so much that, if he takes a liking to someone, he may even take their hand and begin sketching on it. Making art a continued possibility While the Diwali Art Mela offers visitors an opportunity to meet the artists and experience their work, Rashmi hopes the support will continue long after the event. People can purchase original paintings and art-based products, while companies can explore corporate gifting partnerships, commission artwork or organise paid workshops with the artists. The initiative also encourages people to 'adopt an artist' by regularly purchasing a number of their artworks. For Rashmi, the larger goal is to ensure that artistic talent translates into sustained opportunities rather than one-time recognition. "Each artist has their own personality. They are unique. People should know and believe that each is different and that their work deserves to be seen just like that of other artists," she says. This Diwali, as the young artists guide visitors through colours, patterns and abstract forms, they will be doing more than sharing an artistic skill. They will be showing what inclusion can look like when neurodivergent individuals are allowed not just to participate, but to lead. The mela will be held at Gulmohar Park, South Delhi on 31 October and 1 November from 3 pm to 7 pm.

items.title: Ένας πωλητής λαχανικών, μια ανύπαντρη μητέρα και ένα αγόρι από φάρμα: Το «Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye» της SBI Life αναγνωρίζει τις φιλοδοξίες των αθλητών παρα
items.titleOriginal: A Vegetable Seller, a Single Mother and a Farm Boy: SBI Life’s ‘Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye’ Acknowledges the Aspirations of Para Athletes
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο δημοσιεύτηκε σε συνεργασία με την SBI Life Insurance. Η SBI Life Insurance πιστεύει στην απελευθέρωση των ατόμων ώστε να επιδιώξουν τις φιλοδοξίες τους ενώ φροντίζει τα αγαπημένα τους πρόσωπα. Αυτή η πεποίθηση αντανακλάται στη βασική φιλοσοφία της μάρκας, «Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye». Στη Γλασκώβη 2026, τα ταξίδια των παρααθλητών της Ινδίας έφεραν αυτή τη φιλοσοφία…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article has been published in partnership with SBI Life Insurance. SBI Life Insurance believes in liberating individuals to pursue their aspirations while taking care of their loved ones. This belief is reflected in its core brand philosophy, 'Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye'. At Glasgow 2026, the journeys of India's para-athletes brought this philosophy to life, showing how the support of family, coaches and those who stand beside us can make the difference between a dream and a medal. "When I had a polio attack, people forgot that my name was Avinash Kumar. They started calling me Jhandu Kumar, and many laughed at me." For years, Jhandu sold vegetables by the roadside. Whenever he found time, he would borrow a phone and teach himself bodybuilding through YouTube. There was no gym, no formal training and no coach — only a boy who refused to give up on the dream of becoming an athlete. But Jhandu's journey was never his alone. His family supported his ambition, local coaches recognised his potential, and eventually, a national coach gave his talent the direction it needed. But Jhandu's journey was never his alone. His family supported his ambition, local coaches recognised his potential, and eventually, a national coach gave his talent the direction it needed. Photograph: (SBI Life) At Glasgow 2026, that journey culminated in a Commonwealth bronze medal. For Sharmila Dhankar, sport became a way to reclaim a part of herself. "Since childhood, every person dreams of achieving something in life. Some achieve it through academics, while others find success in different fields. It took me 40 years to reach this point. And receiving this medal has given me a new direction in life." For decades, Sharmila put everyone else first — through a difficult marriage and while raising her two daughters on her own. Somewhere along the way, she picked up shot put and found something that was entirely her own. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) At 40, she made history by winning India's first-ever para-athletic gold at the Commonwealth Games. And for Dilip Mahadu Gavit, running began with something much simpler: a childhood love. After losing his right arm in a tree-fall accident at the age of five, Dilip grew up working on farms with one arm. But he never stopped running. When he eventually left his small village and came to the city to run, a coach noticed his speed and invited him to train. At Glasgow 2026, Dilip repaid that faith by winning a record-breaking gold. (Photograph: SBI Life) "I have loved running since childhood. When I came from my small village to the city to run, my coach saw me and asked me to come for training. He said, 'Come and train. We will see what you can do.'" That coach gave Dilip more than training. He brought him from his village and gave him a place to stay in his own home. "Whatever I am today is because of my guru. He brought me from my village and kept me in his own home." At Glasgow 2026, Dilip repaid that faith by winning a record-breaking gold. Three athletes. Three very different journeys. Yet their stories share something powerful: none of them reached the podium alone. Behind Jhandu was a family and coaches who saw an athlete beyond his circumstances. Behind Sharmila was the courage to make space for her own aspirations while carrying the responsibilities of her family. And behind Dilip was a coach who saw potential, opened his home and allowed a young runner to dream bigger. How SBI Life acknowledges dreams This is where SBI Life Insurance's 'Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye' comes to life. The philosophy is built around a simple but powerful idea: our aspirations may be our own, but the journeys that take us towards them are often shaped by the people who stand beside us. SBI Life's partnership with the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) reflects this belief — supporting para-athletes as they pursue excellence, push beyond limitations, and chase bigger dreams. That commitment extends beyond the partnership itself. On 7 September, SBI Life brought together para-athletes at a felicitation event in Delhi, attended by SBI Life's leadership. The event reflected the brand's larger commitment to supporting para-athletes at the grassroots — not simply as a financial services provider, but as a partner invested in their journeys, aspirations and pursuit of excellence. At the event, Amit Jhingram, MD & CEO, SBI Life Insurance, shared, "When the athletes are pursuing their dreams, they put in a lot of hard work with a lot of determination, but it is not only their hard work. It is also the support that their families, their coaches, and their entire ecosystem provide to them. And this is what gels with the philosophy of SBI Life. This is truly "Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye." Despite their vast & different journeys, one thing remains constant: an unwavering determination to pursue their dreams, often strengthened by the support of people and institutions who believe in their potential. (Photograph: SBI Life) For athletes like Jhandu, Sharmila, Dilip and four others – Shilpa Shyla, Mohammed Basil, Soman Rana, Shubham Juyal, a medal represents far more than a moment on the podium. It carries the faith of families, the guidance of coaches, and the support of people who chose to believe in their potential. And that is what makes their victories bigger than individual achievements. "For SBI Life, these athletes are 'Anokhe Heere'. It is a recognition of their achievement, of their success and their story. It's about their determination. It is about their sacrifice," said Ravindra Sharma, EVP and Chief of Brand, Corporate Communications and CSR, SBI Life Insurance. The partnership culminated in Japan But these stories of resilience extended far beyond Glasgow. In October, India's para-athletes competed at the Asian Para Games in Aichi–Nagoya, Japan, bringing a remarkable diversity of experiences from serving in the Indian Army and overcoming life-altering injuries to navigating financial hardships and rediscovering confidence through sport. Despite their vast & different journeys, one thing remained constant: an unwavering determination to pursue their dreams, often strengthened by the support of people and institutions who believe in their potential. This determination resulted in a record-breaking haul of 114 medals for the Indian contingent in Japan. It is this belief in the power of individual aspirations — and in the people who help make them possible — that lies at the heart of SBI Life Insurance's 'Apne Liye, Apno Ke Liye' philosophy. Through this partnership, SBI Life acknowledged the achievements of India's para-athletes, recognising not just the laurels they brought to the nation, but also the resilience, determination and collective support that made these accomplishments possible.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Generates Clean Energy, Saves Land, Improves Fishing—What’s Not to Like? Reading Time: 2 minutes In September 2026, solar developer D3 Energy installed a large solar array, not on land or on a rooftop, but on the surface of a reservoir that serves the water needs of the village of Monroeville, Ohio. This floating power plant covers 12 acres of the reservoir’s 16 acres. If a solar facility of this size, which contains 9,220 solar panels, were built on dry land, it would require 30 acres. So doing it the Monroeville way helps to keep open land available for farming, housing, business or industry, conservation land, or any other use. This 6-megawatt installation is projected to generate about 7,500 megawatt-hours of clean electricity to this village of 1,300 residents. Monroeville has already operated a 4-megawatt ground-mounted solar array, built in 2017. This 10-megawatt total gives the town roughly 13 times as much solar-generated power per capita as the rest of Ohio. Their floating solar array is among the five largest in the U.S. In addition to the clean power produced and the avoidance of using land that might be put toward other needed uses, Floato-voltaics projects such as this one have several other benefits. First, the physical barrier created by the floating platforms significantly reduces water evaporation by blocking direct solar radiation and intercepting wind blowing across the water’s surface. Solar “on the water” thereby reduces evaporation by 30% to 80%, depending on temperatures and humidity in the immediate area. The result, depending upon the size of the floating power plant, is an annual savings of millions of gallons of valuable drinking and irrigation water. Beyond clean power, floating solar arrays like Monroeville’s reduce reservoir water evaporation by 30% to 80% by blocking direct solar radiation and wind, saving millions of gallons of drinking and irrigation water annually. Photo courtesy of D3 Energy . Second, by depriving the water of sunlight, there is a sizable reduction of toxic algal blooms. Photosynthetic organisms like blue-green algae require sunlight to thrive. By heavily shading parts of the reservoir, the concentrations of floating solar panels limit the light penetration needed for massive algal blooms. This naturally improves water quality, reducing expenses from chemical treatments needed to purify the water. Third, more fish. During the warmer months, the floating platforms insulate the reservoir’s water against seasonal temperature spikes, helping support cold-water fish species. Local reservoirs are often favorite local fishing spots. And fourth, cleaning issues. Land-based solar arrays, whether in farming or more urbanized areas, often deal with dust, dirt, and other airborne debris. For best panel performance, cleaning of their surfaces in these situations is advisable. Open bodies of water are inherently less affected by blowing dirt and dust, keeping the panels cleaner longer and reducing maintenance costs. All things considered, with all the bodies of fresh water dotting the planet, maybe we should all look more closely for floato-voltaic opportunities just beyond our own backyard. The post Generates Clean Energy, Saves Land, Improves Fishing—What’s Not to Like? appeared first on Happy Eco News .
