items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Renewable Natural Gas Is Turning Everyday Waste Into Cleaner Fuel for Businesses Reading Time: 3 minutes Renewable Natural Gas Is Turning Everyday Waste Into Cleaner Fuel for Businesses The shift towards sustainability has led to numerous innovations in the way that companies operate. One of the most exciting developments is the use of renewable natural gas (RNG). RNG is created by capturing methane from sources such as agricultural runoff, landfills, and wastewater treatment plants. This not only reduces the amount of greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere but also creates a new source of energy for those facilities. Adding RNG to your natural gas procurement for businesses is a straightforward way to hit green targets without risking downtime. It tackles organic waste head-on and acts as an easy, drop-in replacement for fossil fuels. How Everyday Waste Transforms into Power The journey from refuse to resource is a fascinating one that involves the capture and processing of methane gas from decomposing organic matter before it escapes into the atmosphere. Instead of allowing this potent greenhouse gas to contribute to climate change, facilities that use anaerobic digesters are able to break down dairy manure, food scraps, and wastewater sludge. The biogas that is produced from these facilities undergoes a purification process to remove moisture, carbon dioxide, and other elements from the gas. The resulting gas is structurally identical to natural gas, allowing it to be injected into existing gas infrastructure and utilized by commercial fleets and manufacturing plants without any need for modification to their equipment. Evaluating the Financial and Environmental Dual Benefits Shifting to this circular energy model offers companies a unique opportunity to tackle two major corporate objectives simultaneously: minimizing ecological impact and stabilizing operational costs. Because RNG is domestically produced from continuous waste streams, it can help shield commercial consumers from the extreme price volatility often associated with global fossil fuel markets. When executives sit down to analyze their overall natural gas procurement strategies, incorporating a renewable component proves highly advantageous for long-term budget forecasting. Furthermore, utilizing this upgraded biogas significantly lowers a company’s direct carbon footprint, allowing brands to authentically market their sustainability achievements to an increasingly eco-conscious consumer base. Overcoming Adoption Barriers and Infrastructure Myths One of the most common misconceptions about the implementation of alternative fuels is that companies will have to invest millions of dollars into new machinery and infrastructure. However, since the upgraded biomethane is chemically identical to the geological methane that now fuels the majority of the nation’s cities and industries, the fuel can be easily implemented into the existing pipeline system without any need for the implementation of new machinery or infrastructure. Also, since the fuel is chemically identical to the existing fuel, the implementation of this new fuel source will not require the implementation of new infrastructure. Instead, the companies can simply update their purchasing agreements with the companies that produce the fuel to implement the new fuel source into their operations. Strategic Sourcing for Corporate Sustainability Goals A sophisticated strategy is needed to source sustainable energy, especially given the growing demand for environmentally friendly substitutes in a number of heavy industries. To make sure they are obtaining genuine environmental attributes in addition to their physical fuel supply, corporate buyers must negotiate a complicated web of producers, marketers, and local utility regulations. When handling natural gas procurement for businesses, look for suppliers who can trace their biomethane straight from the farm or landfill to your facility. Securing these transparent contracts makes it much easier to prove emission cuts to stakeholders and meet strict climate regulations. Embracing the Circular Economy of Tomorrow Another way in which the use of upgraded biogas can benefit commercial enterprises is in reducing their reliance on traditional fossil fuels. The use of biogas as a fuel source for these companies can help to significantly reduce their carbon footprint without any changes to their daily operations. As the technology to capture and refine methane improves, the availability and affordability of biogas will continue to increase. Companies that incorporate biogas into their energy portfolios will be at an advantage compared to their competitors who do not take such steps towards sustainability. items.descriptionOriginal: Compostable plastics are touted as a greener alternative to conventional petroleum-based plastics that can linger in the environment for centuries. But there’s a catch. Degradable plastics only break down in the right conditions typically found in a composting facility. The tons of compostable plastic that ends up in oceans can still float around for decades and threaten marine life and ecosystems. Researchers have found a way for plastics to break down much faster in the ocean. They embedded tiny amounts of plastic-degrading enzymes in compostable polyester plastics. The enzyme-containing polyesters completely degraded in a relatively short time period even in microbe-scarce environments. The method works at all depths from coastal waters to the deep open sea, the researchers report in the journal Nature . There are many types of biodegradable plastics in commercial use today. These plastics are designed to decompose completely by microorganisms at certain temperatures and humidities . Those conditions are found in industrial composting facilities and with more care in backyard compost settings. But out in cold ocean water, biodegradable plastics can persist for a long time. The research team from Japan took four types of compostable plastic—PBS, PBSA, PCL, and PBAT—and melted them. The heat of the melt would destroy plastic-degrading enzymes . So the researchers made freeze-dried forms of Candida antarctica lipase B and Humicola insolens cutinase enzymes. items.descriptionOriginal: On a polluted day, the air can look like a grey haze hanging over a city, obscuring buildings and making every breath feel heavier. But what if some of that pollution could be collected, transformed and given a new purpose — not as waste, but as a material used to build our homes and workplaces? Mumbai-based architect Tejas Sidnal is exploring precisely that possibility. Through his startup, Carbon Craft Design, he is turning recovered black carbon into architectural tiles, giving a second life to a pollutant while rethinking how building materials are made. The idea took shape when Sidnal, while studying architecture, became fascinated by biomimicry — the practice of drawing inspiration from nature to solve human problems. He began questioning what truly makes a society healthy, looking beyond grand buildings to the essentials of clean air, water and food. The startup combines recovered carbon with cement, recycled marble powder and marble chips to create its signature Carbon Tiles. Photograph: ( Architecture + Desig n) This led him to a contradiction: the construction industry itself contributes significantly to global carbon emissions, yet the materials used to create our built environment are rarely viewed through the lens of pollution. Could the very carbon waste contributing to the problem become part of the solution? In 2020, Sidnal launched Carbon Craft Design to turn this question into a tangible innovation: Carbon Tiles. How does carbon waste become a tile? Black carbon is produced by the incomplete combustion of fuels and other carbon-rich materials. When released into the atmosphere, it contributes to air pollution and climate change. Carbon Craft Design sources recovered carbon waste from industrial processes, including tyre recycling and factory pyrolysis . The material is cleaned and processed before being blended with cement, recycled marble powder and marble chips. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Anuj Mohanty (@anujmohanty_) The mixture is then compressed using hydraulic presses to create tiles with distinctive geometric patterns. Unlike conventional ceramic tiles, which typically require energy-intensive firing in high-temperature kilns, Carbon Tiles are compressed and allowed to set at room temperature. According to the startup, this manufacturing process uses around one-fifth of the energy required to make conventional fired tiles. The company also states that every square metre of its tiles prevents the equivalent of 25 kg of carbon dioxide emissions. Made using hydraulic presses and set at room temperature, Carbon Tiles avoid the energy-intensive firing process used for conventional ceramic tiles. Photograph: ( Wallparer ) By incorporating recovered carbon into a durable building material, the startup aims to give waste a useful destination instead of allowing it to contribute to the pollution burden. A little science, a little craft & a lot of creativity For Sidnal, sustainability is not just about developing a new material. It is also about rethinking how products are made and who gets to make them. Carbon Craft Design collaborates with ceramic artisans in Morbi, Gujarat, a region known for its tile-making industry. Drawing on traditional craftsmanship, the artisans handcraft the tiles' distinctive geometric patterns, bringing character and detail to the material. Carbon Craft Design collaborates with ceramic artisans in Morbi, Gujarat, to create geometric tile patterns that combine traditional craftsmanship with material innovation. Photograph: ( Carbon Craft Design ) This partnership brings together material research and established craft skills. The recovered carbon and low-energy manufacturing process address environmental concerns, while the artisans' expertise helps create tiles suited to contemporary architectural spaces. The result is a product that places sustainability alongside aesthetics — an important consideration in an industry where materials must be functional as well as visually appealing. From an architect's ideas to showrooms Turning an environmental concept into a commercially viable product requires more than a promising material. It needs customers willing to use it, too. Carbon Craft Design has worked with major brands, including Adidas, creating tile patterns for its showrooms. Such projects demonstrate how recycled materials can find a place in commercial interiors, where design and durability matter alongside sustainability. Carbon Craft Design has created custom tile patterns for Adidas showrooms, bringing recycled materials into commercial spaces. Photograph: ( Carbon Craft Design ) The startup has also received support from impact investors, including Social Alpha and the Pilani Innovation Entrepreneurship Development Society, and participated in climate-focused accelerators. Its recognitions include the Lexus Design Award India in 2020 and the No Waste Challenge, organised by What Design Can Do and the IKEA Foundation, in 2021. These milestones reflect a growing interest in materials that rethink the traditional journey from resource extraction to manufacturing and disposal. Could the buildings of tomorrow be made from today's waste? No single material can solve the climate crisis. Construction must continue to address emissions across its supply chains, energy use and building lifecycles, while innovations such as Carbon Tiles must demonstrate their durability, safety and environmental benefits at scale. But Sidnal's work offers a tangible starting point. By recovering carbon waste, reducing the energy used in tile manufacturing and working with traditional artisans, Carbon Craft Design brings together pollution management, sustainable production and local craftsmanship. Carbon Craft Design shows how recovered carbon waste can be transformed into durable building materials, rethinking how the spaces we inhabit are made. Photograph: ( Carbon Craft Design ) The idea is both simple and powerful: something that once contributed to an environmental problem can become part of the spaces people inhabit every day. And perhaps that is where a cleaner future begins — not only by preventing waste, but by learning to see its potential before it is discarded. Sources: 'Tejas Jindal' by Indian Diaspora 'Tejas Sidnal' by What Design Can Do Carbon Craft Design

items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine having to walk more than a kilometre every time you need to bring home drinking water. On a hot summer day, even filling a few pots can mean a tiring journey, with no guarantee that there will be enough water for everyone at home. For years, this was a reality for families in Wadji, a village in Maharashtra's Washim district. Residents travelled up to 1.5 km to fetch drinking water, a struggle made harder during the summer months when water sources became scarce. But what if the answer to their water problem was all around them, quite literally, in the air they breathe? That is the idea behind Meghdoot, a machine that draws moisture from the air and turns it into drinking water. Installed in Wadji, the technology can produce up to 500 litres of purified water a day, offering the village a new source of water without having to rely entirely on wells or groundwater. Even a pot of drinking water meant a long walk Wadji, home to nearly 2,000 people, is among the communities in Vidarbha grappling with water scarcity. The challenge extends beyond the village. According to Central Ground Water Board reports, nearly 40 villages in Risod taluka fall under the semi-critical groundwater category. For years, residents of Wadji village in Maharashtra walked up to 1.5 km to fetch drinking water. Photograph: ( Frontline ) For residents, the problem becomes particularly difficult during summer, when temperatures rise, and reliable access to drinking water becomes harder to secure. To address this, the Wadji Gram Panchayat adopted a technology that draws on a resource people rarely think of as a source of drinking water: the moisture present in the air. The village is reported to be the first and only one in Maharashtra to have adopted this technology. How does the technology turn air into water? The system, called Meghdoot, uses Atmospheric Water Generation technology to extract moisture from the air and convert it into liquid water. The process begins with fans drawing humid air into the machine. Filters remove airborne particles such as dust and pollen before a refrigeration-based mechanism cools the air to its dew point. As the air cools, water vapour condenses into droplets, much like moisture forming on the outside of a cold glass. Developed by CSIR-IICT scientists in Hyderabad in collaboration with Maithri Aquatech, Meghdoot offers an alternative source of drinking water. Photograph: ( Maithri Aquatech ) The collected water then undergoes further purification. Activated carbon filtration, ultraviolet (UV) disinfection and other treatment processes help make it suitable for drinking. The purified water is stored before being made available for consumption. The unit has a reported capacity of around 500 litres a day. However, actual output from atmospheric water generators can depend on conditions such as humidity and temperature, as well as the machine's operation. Unlike conventional sources that draw directly on groundwater or surface water, this approach collects moisture from the atmosphere. It can therefore provide an additional source of drinking water in places where existing supplies are under pressure. The Hyderabad scientists and villagers behind Wadji's water innovation The technology was developed by scientists at the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-Indian Institute of Chemical Technology (CSIR-IICT) in Hyderabad, in collaboration with Maithri Aquatech. Key contributors to the project include Dr Sridhar, Dr Nivedita Sahu and their team. The system was procured with support from CSIR-IICT under the guidance of its then director, Dr Chandrasekhar. At the village level, the Wadji Gram Panchayat took the initiative to bring the technology to the community. The unit has been installed at the Zilla Parishad Primary School and Anganwadi, making drinking water accessible at locations used by children and local residents. Installed at Wadji's Zilla Parishad Primary School and Anganwadi, the unit brings drinking water closer to children and local residents. Photograph: ( NDTV ) Its placement at these institutions also gives schoolchildren and Anganwadi attendees an opportunity to benefit from a source of drinking water close to where they spend part of their day. Could this help other villages facing water shortages? Atmospheric water generation is not a substitute for groundwater conservation, rainwater harvesting or reliable public water infrastructure. The technology also requires electricity, and its output depends on local atmospheric conditions. Its long-term usefulness will depend on operating costs, maintenance and consistent performance. By drawing moisture from the air, Meghdoot offers Wadji residents an alternative source of drinking water amid growing water scarcity. Photograph: (Outlook India) For Wadji, the promise of Meghdoot lies in something simple: bringing drinking water closer to the people who need it. What once required a journey of a kilometre or more could now be met, in part, by a machine that draws moisture from the air. While the technology cannot replace long-term solutions such as groundwater conservation and rainwater harvesting, it offers another way to address water shortages. If maintained well and adapted to local conditions, such innovations could help more communities explore alternative sources of drinking water, one village at a time. Source: 'When wells run dry, Vidarbha's Wadji literally taps drinking water from air' : by Bhaskar Mehare for The Times Of India, Published on 13 June 2026. 'Video: Drinking water from the humidity in the air! Innovative experiment by Gram Panchayat' : by Loksatta, Published on 13 June 2026.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Removing Forever Chemicals from Farmlands Gets Easier with New Eco-Friendly, Affordable Method Reading Time: 3 minutes A new Yale-led study finds that removing forever chemicals from farmlands could become far cheaper using hemp, rock dust, and biochar, potentially cleaning contaminated soils within a decade. Removing Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) from farmlands could soon become far cheaper and far less destructive. A new Yale-led study outlines a three-step process using plants, rock dust, and biochar. Researchers say it could work within a single decade. The chemicals in question are often called “forever chemicals.” They resist breaking down and have built up in soil for decades. Much of that contamination traces back to sewage sludge once used as fertilizer. Removing forever chemicals from farmlands matters because these chemicals do not simply fade away on their own. Once present in soil, they can persist for generations without intervention. That persistence is part of why the chemicals earned their nickname in the first place. The study estimates PFAS have contaminated roughly 1.2 million hectares of U.S. cropland. Some Maine farms have already shut down after soil tests exceeded safety limits. Exposure to these chemicals has been linked to certain cancers, thyroid problems, and fertility issues. Health researchers have also linked long-term PFAS exposure to weakened immune response. These risks make removing forever chemicals from farmland a public health priority, not just an environmental one. Farmers directly exposed to contaminated soil and water face some of the highest risks. Conventional cleanup methods of removing forever chemicals from farmlands usually means excavating and burning contaminated soil entirely. That approach can cost an estimated $1.6 million per hectare. Scaled nationally, the total bill could reach roughly $8 trillion. The Yale team’s model instead starts with basalt rock dust spread across farmland. This dust shifts soil pH in a way that sounds counterproductive at first. It actually makes PFAS more available for uptake by nearby plants. Hemp and certain perennial grasses then draw the loosened PFAS out of the soil. Rock dust sped up removal of one compound, called PFOS, by 20-40%. Researchers call PFOS the higher regulatory priority of the two chemicals studied. Harvested plants next go through a heating process to make biochar. That heat destroys much of the remaining chemical structure left in the plant tissue. Spreading the finished biochar back onto contaminated fields could cut chemical runoff by 95%. A Yale-developed process for removing forever chemicals from farmlands uses basalt rock dust to loosen chemical bonds in contaminated soil, allowing hemp (photo above) and perennial grasses to draw pollutants up through their roots before harvesting and heating the plants into biochar that, spread back onto fields, could cut PFAS runoff by 95%. Photo by Mark Stebnicki on Pexels. Postdoctoral researcher Jake Thompson led the study alongside professor Noah Planavsky at Yale. Planavsky, who comes from a farming family, says farmers urgently need better tools to address this problem. Thompson notes that small and organic farms were often hit hardest by past PFAS-laden fertilizer use. Combined, researchers project these steps could bring soils below safety thresholds within a decade. Estimated costs come in at around $1,460 per hectare each year. That figure is a tiny fraction of traditional excavation and burning costs. The rock dust and biochar processes also carry an added climate benefit. Both methods help pull carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere over time. Scaled nationwide, researchers estimate the approach could remove 10.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide each year. Unlike excavation, this method would let farmers keep working their land throughout the process. Researchers note that removing forever chemicals from farmlands is a global issue beyond the United States. In parts of Europe and the UK, most sewage sludge still gets applied directly to farmland. Europe alone spreads about 10 million tons of sewage sludge onto cropland each year. The United Kingdom applies sludge to roughly 70% of its farmland. China follows a similar pattern, researchers say, making the contamination problem a shared one worldwide. So far, the findings come from computer modeling built on real farm data rather than full field trials. The research team now hopes to test the approach on partner farms across different soil types. Real-world results of removing forever chemicals from farmlands through this approach will show whether these modeled gains hold up outside the lab. If they do, hemp, rock dust, and biochar could offer struggling farmers a genuine way forward. For land written off as unusable, that alone would count as real progress. The post Removing Forever Chemicals from Farmlands Gets Easier with New Eco-Friendly, Affordable Method appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Th…
items.descriptionOriginal: I n 1991, Saskia Sassen published The Global City in which she asserted that London had more in common with New York and Tokyo than it did with other parts of the U.K. The geography of culture wasn’t delineated by national borders, she argued — there was no need to travel across an ocean to experience ways of life vastly different from your own. That ethos is embodied by American Exchange Project, an intercultural exchange program for youth that takes place entirely within the United States. The exchanges send students who have just graduated high school on weeklong sojourns to U.S. communities completely different from their own. Participating students then host a cohort of peers in their own town, creating a true interchange of American experiences. For many of these students, the exchange is not only an opportunity to see a different part of the country, but to have deep discussions with their new friends about how their lives are different — and the same. “I hadn’t really experienced something where the point of spending time together was to talk about this big, deep stuff,” says Alden Swanson, a student from Chestertown, Maryland whose exchange took place in Orem, Utah. “And that led to so many interesting conversations about differences, but also brought up a lot of similarities about beliefs and how we thought about the world.” Interactions like these are becoming rarer, as Americans increasingly choose to live in cities and towns where their neighbors hold views similar to their own. According to Bill Bishop, author of The Big Sort: Why the Clustering of Like-Minded America Is Tearing Us Apart , the share of voters living in “landslide counties” — where a presidential candidate won by 20 or more points — rose from about 26 percent in 1976 to more than 60 percent in 2016. People are proactively moving to communities with less political and cultural heterogeneity. More than two out of five Americans consider it important that their neighbors share their politics, according to Bishop. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] That said, American Exchange Project makes it clear that these exchanges aren’t about exposing students to new political views (any more than a foreign exchange program would primarily be about politics). Instead, they’re a rare opportunity to immerse young people in an unfamiliar American context and help them build empathy for those whose communities and cultures diverge from their own. Sunny Beam, a student from Ilwaco, Washington, had never spent time in a place with a population of more than 10,000 people before her exchange sent her to the Bronx in New York City. “It’s not even comparable to the places I lived before. It was so nice,” she says. “You’d think that living in a small town, everyone’s super closely knit together, but that’s not always a good thing.” The culture shock of being transported from small town to booming metropolis was offset by the hospitality she was shown by a city used to embracing people of all stripes. Alden Swanson and some of her American Exchange Project peers. Courtesy of Alden Swanson “Because everyone didn’t know everyone else, you would think that they’d be super-standoffish, but everyone was just incredibly welcoming, even to strangers,” she says. “It felt more community-based than my town because everyone was so welcoming and everyone was so willing to, like, work with the diversity rather than shut people out.” For Andrew Wood from Kilgore, Texas, who was also sent to New York, one of the biggest lessons of the exchange was that connecting across cultures needn’t be complicated. “I’m a person who likes to bring the group together,” says Wood. “And so as soon as we got there, I’m like, ‘Okay, guys, you want to play some UNO? Because they got UNO cards for us.’ And so we decided to play UNO, and we started talking and getting to know each other, and we kind of just really clicked from there.” The post The Student Exchange Program That Never Leaves the U.S. appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Study Reveals Primates Forming Cross-Species Friendships with Dogs, Deer, and Pigs Worldwide Reading Time: 3 minutes An international review documents 427 cases of primates forming cross-species friendships. Why do humans keep pets? A new study led by researchers at the University of Oxford and collaborators worldwide suggests the behavioral foundations of human-animal companionship may not be unique to humans. The team compiled the first comprehensive review of friendly interactions between nonhuman primates and other species, documenting 427 cases involving 88 primate species and 127 partner species, 55 of them non-primates. Published in the journal Primates, the study draws together evidence spanning several decades, from the 1970s through 2025, combining 303 cases from scientific literature, 58 cases from screened photographs and videos, and 66 cases collected through a global survey of primatologists. Together, these sources produced 204 distinct species pairings, making this the most comprehensive overview to date of cross-species social behavior among monkeys and apes. The diversity documented among primates forming cross-species friendships proved remarkable. Partner species included sheep, tapirs, deer, domestic pigs, cats, and dogs, as well as owls, lizards, toads, and even insects. Play and grooming emerged as the most common behaviors, recorded in 139 and 136 cases, respectively, but researchers also found primates carrying, huddling, sharing food with, and occasionally adopting individuals from entirely different species. One of the most striking and now well-documented examples of primates forming cross-species friendships involves Japanese macaques in Yakushima, Japan, who groom and ride on the backs of sika deer, repeatedly interacting peacefully over long periods. In China’s Yunnan Golden Monkey National Park, researchers observed a young black-and-white snub-nosed monkey playing on the back of a domestic pig. Elsewhere, a langur was seen attentively stroking a squirrel, a silverback gorilla carefully cradled a tiny wild bushbaby, and a bonobo gently held a mongoose pup. Domestic dogs appeared repeatedly throughout the review, with researchers recording 26 wild or free-ranging encounters involving dogs. Rhesus macaques and dogs formed one of the most frequently reported species pairings in the entire dataset, suggesting these interactions represent more than isolated curiosities. Most interactions among primates forming cross-species friendships occurred between closely related species with similar bodies, gestures, and social habits, animals that may find it easier to interpret one another without conflict. Yet evolutionary distance proved far from an insurmountable barrier. Age and sex patterns emerged clearly across the dataset: juvenile and infant monkeys were significantly more likely to initiate play than grooming, while adult females showed the opposite pattern, favoring grooming behaviors instead. Researchers suggest play may offer young primates a flexible, low-stakes way to test an unfamiliar partner’s temperament. A chase, a leap, or a playful climb can quickly reveal whether another animal responds with tolerance, enthusiasm, or aggression, information valuable before investing in a longer social bond. Notably, unlike many mixed-species groupings found in nature, these friendships did not appear to provide obvious survival advantages such as improved access to food or protection from predators. Instead, the animals frequently played together, groomed one another, carried each other, or simply rested side by side, behaviors suggesting that primates forming cross-species friendships reflect genuine curiosity and social flexibility extending well beyond mere practical necessity. Primates forming cross-species friendships suggest curiosity and social flexibility rather than a survival advantage, with juveniles more likely to initiate play while adult females favored grooming behaviors instead. Photos by (a) Nicholas Chapoy, (b) Sabit Hasan, (c) Senthi Aathavan Senthilverl, and (d) Neil Challis, courtesy of Primates . Not every interaction ended positively. Curiosity and caregiving occasionally tipped into rough handling, and researchers recorded 13 cases in which a partner animal died, with victims including birds, pangolins, a domestic cat, and other primates. In one striking example, a male baboon in Saudi Arabia appeared to have kidnapped a domestic puppy, carrying it around for extended periods. Beyond illuminating the possible origins of human-animal companionship, researchers believe these findings carry meaningful implications for conservation and animal welfare. Understanding why certain species readily form positive relationships with others could help improve management of mixed-species environments, from wildlife sanctuaries to zoos housing multiple species in shared enclosures. The sheer range of documented behavior suggests that primates forming cross-species friendships is far more widespread than scientists had previously realized, indicating that social lives among monkeys and apes extend well beyond their own species boundaries. While these animals are not keeping pets in the deliberate, sustained way humans do today, their behaviors may represent early evolutionary building blocks eventually giving rise to the caregiving instincts and cross-species companionship that define humanity’s relationship with domesticated animals. The post Study Reveals Primates Forming Cross-Species Friendships with Dogs, Deer, and Pigs Worldwide appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A small orchard planted 13 years ago at a shuttered Kansas CIty elementary school has grown into a national movement that has inspired more than 847 orchards with 14,000 trees in 17 cities, all producing fruit for people living within walking distance. Kansas City itself now has 248 free orchards, with almost 4,600 fruit, nut and berry trees, more than any other US city. After a community gardening group in St. Louis asked for help almost a decade ago, the Giving Grove expanded into cities from Seattle to Atlanta, and is in talks with San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York City. "It's stuff people can learn, but it takes a long time, and it's not really efficient for one group to do that," said founder Kevin Birzer. "So our thought from day one was we would provide that expertise, the knowledge of how to grow the trees, how to select the trees." The Giving Grove helps local groups find grant money, improve soil, prune trees, and work with volunteer orchard stewards. Much of its budget comes from 1% for the Planet, which mobilizes businesses to direct 1% of their annual revenue to vetted environmental solutions.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM As temperatures drop, bugs start looking for the same thing you do: somewhere warmer. If you’ve been reaching for the vinegar bottle as a first line of defense, you’re not alone. It’s an easy instinct: vinegar seems safe, familiar, and you probably already have some under the sink. Two pest management experts say the results tend to disappoint, though. Greg Baumann , founding partner of Pest Control Warrior, and Garrett Thrasher , co-owner and general manager at Thrasher Pest Control, both say vinegar works on a narrower range of pests than most people expect, and mostly not in the way people tend to use it. Where it works, and where it doesn’t Thrasher says a wet vinegar spray applied directly to a soft-bodied insect will usually kill on contact. Pantry moths, caterpillars, and mosquitoes are vulnerable to it. But vinegar evaporates quickly, and once it’s dry it does nothing to stop cockroaches, beetles, spiders, or ants. Baumann cites peer-reviewed university research showing it has negligible effects on most common household insects. “ Pests will happily walk on [wet surfaces] after vinegar evaporates,” Baumann says. “The homeowner might think it is still on the surface because the odor lingers in the air.” There’s also a surface damage problem. The acidity can strip paint finishes and stain baseboards when applied along window frames and door trim. If you want a DIY option before calling a professional, Thrasher recommends diatomaceous earth over vinegar. What the experts recommend instead Sealing works better than spraying. Caulking windows, weatherstripping doors, and adding door sweeps close off the most common entry points. Attics and crawlspaces need the same treatment. For active pest pressure around entry points, an outdoor insecticide labeled for the specific pest and location will hold up longer. Check the label to confirm it covers the right conditions for where you’re applying it. A quick walk around doors and windows once a week catches problems early, before they get in. And if you collect acorns or pine cones this fall, Thrasher recommends 30 minutes in a 150-degree Fahrenheit oven before bringing them inside. It kills any insects hiding inside them. If pests are already getting in, a professional can inspect for openings and seal them. Many pest control companies now work with low-impact products, so going professional doesn’t have to mean bringing in something harsh. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Το πρόγραμμα ονομάζεται Thamani Asili , που σημαίνει…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Kenya committed $160 million over ten years to protect 173,000 square kilometers (roughly 67,000 square miles, or 17.3 million hectares) across some of the least-disturbed land in Africa: the Great Rift Valley, the Maasai Mara, and surrounding biodiversity areas. The program is called Thamani Asili , which means “value of nature” in Kiswahili. Funding splits evenly: $80 million from the Kenyan government, $80 million from dozens of private donors, including billionaire heirs to the Walton and Cargill family fortunes. The money flows through a Project Finance for Permanence (PFP) model, which ties disbursements to verifiable government policy changes rather than goodwill commitments. Four focus zones The initiative will start in four geographic areas. Tsavo, Kenya’s largest national park complex, holds 40 percent of the country’s elephants and 20 percent of its critically endangered black rhinos. A southern zone along the Tanzanian border spans the Maasai Mara and links into the Serengeti, a corridor that wildlife has used for seasonal migration long before either country drew its borders. The Great Rift Valley and two additional hotspots round out the four. What PFP requires Conservation funding has a recurring problem: it arrives, gets spent, and produces little that changes policy or land status. The PFP model is a structural attempt to fix that. Money is conditional on the government hitting specific policy benchmarks, not delivered up front. Brazil and Gabon signed similar agreements last year. Namibia and Botswana are in the works. Kenya’s deal is among the largest yet. Closing the 30×30 gap Kenya has committed to the global “30×30” target: 30 percent of land and sea protected by 2030. The Nature Conservancy puts current coverage at 20 to 23 percent. Ryan Bidwell, who runs TNC’s PFP program, said this deal would largely close the distance. The economic case is also there. A UN Environment Programme report drew on Kenyan government data showing that roughly 42 percent of the country’s GDP and 70 percent of its employment depend on nature in some form. Cabinet Secretary for Tourism and Wildlife Rebecca Miano said the program would benefit both wildlife and the farming communities that work these landscapes. “There is a substantial gap that would be largely closed,” Bidwell said. Whether it closes depends on Kenya delivering on the policy commitments the funding is tied to, something that’s far harder to sidestep under PFP than under a conventional grant. Η τόσο απαραίτητη ενημέρωση προέρχεται από την American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, Am…
items.descriptionOriginal: Another exciting step forward for women’s health: Four major health societies teamed up to create the first shared framework and clinical guidance for women’s heart health, tailored to distinct life phases — from first menstruation to postmenopause. The much-needed update comes from the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. Because while cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death in women, medical research has historically centered on men’s symptoms and physiology (which differ from women in myriad ways), thus reducing the quality of care women receive on average. This landmark move seeks to change that. The new framework organizes women’s cardiovascular care into four chronological life stages that account for hormonal and biological transitions, plus pregnancy. In addition to getting clinicians on the same page about women’s cardiovascular health, the system and its accompanying guidance can help them identify risks earlier and take necessary action before problems worsen. https://iprsoftwaremedia.com/67/files/20269/07b6ae0ca5d8a720af4942e310f02184/Dr.%20Khan%20on%20whole%20life%20view%20of%20womens%20heart%20health.mp4 “Women experience their health care across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” Dr. Sadiya S. Khan, chair of the collaborative writing group and professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, said in a news release. She noted that the updates, a trio of scientific papers published this week, “connect the dots” for providers across health domains, so holistic care can begin in adolescence. Khan added that the approach emphasizes that cardiovascular health can’t be fully understood by looking only at the heart. “We need to recognize that women’s heart health is deeply interconnected with hormonal and emotional health,” she said. The Stages Stage 1: Perimenarche The first stage comprises the transition that occurs around the first menstrual period, generally taking place between ages 8 and 15. In an essay for Time , Khan wrote that a first period before age 10 can serve as a signal of higher cardiovascular risk. “Heart health begins long before adulthood,” Dr. Amanda Marma Perak, vice-chair of the collaborative writing group and a pediatric cardiologist at Lurie Children’s Hospital, added in the news release. “As pediatric clinicians, we have the opportunity to help every girl start strong and to ensure that what we learn about her health follows her as she grows.” Stage 2: Ovarian Cycling This stage represents the approximate ages of 15-44, when regular ovulation and hormone cycles are established. Pregnancy most often occurs during these years. “Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) can frequently disrupt sleep, physical activity, and eating patterns, which are relevant to cardiovascular health,” Khan wrote for Time. “These symptoms are common, but being common does not make them inconsequential.” Heavy or irregular bleeding can also act as indicators. Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (formerly known as PCOS), for example, has been associated with a significant increase in risk for heart disease. Stage 3: Perimenopause Stage 3 represents the transition from regular to variable cycles, skipped periods, and hormone changes, taking place around ages 45-51. “Recognizing perimenopause as a distinct life stage acknowledges that its symptoms can disrupt daily life, persist for years, and deserve treatment,” wrote Khan. “Hormone and nonhormonal treatments can help, with decisions guided by symptoms, age, cardiovascular and cancer history, and a woman’s preferences. The same visit offers an opportunity to assess cardiovascular disease risk and address changes in cholesterol and cardiometabolic health.” Stage 4: Postmenopause Representing the years following menopause, which begins 12 months after one’s final period, this stage can account for 40% of a woman’s life. It occurs at approximately 51 years and older. The news release notes that most heart attacks, strokes, and heart-failure events occur during this stage — but are more than 80% preventable when steps are taken early. Pregnancy (in Any Life Stage) The framework identifies the time before, during, and after pregnancy “as a biological ‘stress test’ that can identify cardiovascular risks that may have been previously unrecognized,” per the release, which highlights postpartum care as a “missed opportunity” for many women. “Only about 60% of U.S. women with high blood pressure-related complications during pregnancy receive follow-up care for their high blood pressure within six months of delivery,” it states, noting that the American Heart Association is calling for immediate action to address that gap. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” Khan said. “Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Reading Time: 3 minutes Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Replacing a car is a big decision. Replacing two familiar journeys can be a smaller, more useful experiment. An e-bike may suit a trip to work, a grocery pickup, or a visit to the library without needing to handle every journey in your week. The starting question is not “How far can this bike go?” It is “Which journeys can I repeat comfortably, legally, and with a workable backup?” This checklist helps turn that question into a practical plan rather than a promise about distance, money, or carbon savings. 1. Define the two trips you want to replace Look at an ordinary week and choose journeys you currently make by car. Start with predictable destinations, manageable loads, and flexible arrival times. An appointment with no margin for delay is probably not the easiest first attempt. Be clear about counting: an outward journey and its return are two one-way trips, but one round-trip outing. Write down which definition you are using. Two bike rides do not necessarily replace two car journeys if someone still drives the same route to collect you or your shopping. 2. Find the calmer route, not just the shortest Compare a cycling map with your knowledge of local streets. Look for lower-traffic connections, suitable crossings, and routes where you feel comfortable managing the bike. A small detour may be worthwhile if it avoids a difficult junction. Inspect the awkward details: where does a bike lane end, how do you cross a busy road, and is the destination entrance accessible? Check current local rules for your bike’s class and the roads or paths you plan to use. An app’s suggested route is not proof that access is legal or conditions are suitable. 3. Budget door-to-door time Allow time to unlock the bike, load bags, negotiate crossings, park, and get ready at your destination. Do not base your schedule on the motor’s assistance cutoff or a brief top-speed reading. Neither tells you the average speed of an entire journey. Try the route without an important deadline. Record the complete travel time and how it felt, then add a buffer appropriate to your schedule. 4. Plan battery use for the whole outing Include the return leg, any errands, and a reasonable detour. Advertised maximum range is not a dependable prediction for your route. Hills, wind, temperature, assistance level, load, battery condition, and other factors can change consumption. Begin with short, familiar rides and note battery use under your own conditions. Leave a conservative reserve rather than planning to arrive empty. If charging at work is part of the plan, confirm permission and a suitable location first. Follow the bike and battery manufacturer’s charging instructions; do not assume any available charger is compatible. 5. Solve parking and carrying before leaving Know where you can lock the bike at both ends. Check whether the parking arrangement works with the frame, your lock, and the property’s rules. If stairs or lifting are involved, assess whether you can manage the bike safely before relying on that access. Pack a realistic load for a practice ride. Secure bags so they cannot interfere with steering, wheels, or braking, and respect the bike’s and rack’s stated limits. Check tire condition and pressure, brakes, lights, and load security before departure. A lighter shopping trip may be a better starting point than a weekly household shop. For a practical example focused on weekend outings, FavoriteBikes’ guide to planning e-bike errands covers stop order, bags, cargo balance, and battery margin. Adapt those planning ideas to the trips you actually want to replace. 6. Decide when not to ride Choose your fallback before you need it. Transit, rescheduling, a lift, or using the car may be appropriate when conditions exceed your ability or the bike’s limits. Check transit rules in advance, including restrictions on e-bikes, batteries, and available carrying space. Rain, darkness, strong winds, snow, and ice can change the decision. Clothing and equipment do not make every route safe, and motor assistance does not remove traction or braking risks. Avoid an unsuitable route rather than treating two weekly trips as a target that must be met regardless of conditions. 7. Keep a simple two-week record For each attempt, note the journey replaced, door-to-door time, battery use, load, conditions, and any difficulty. Include the days you chose not to ride. Those decisions help reveal whether the plan works beyond an unusually easy day. If you compare costs, distinguish avoided fuel or parking from car expenses you still pay, and include relevant bike costs. Do not assign a fixed emissions saving to every ride: the result depends on the vehicle journey actually displaced and the comparison being made. Keep the routes that fit your life, revise the difficult ones, and leave room for other transport. The useful outcome is a repeatable choice—not a perfect score or a commitment to give up the car. The post Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News When Humans Rise, Must Another Life Fall? Rethinking Human Interests and Animal Flourishing in an Anthropocentric World Reading Time: 4 minutes If human beings rise, must other life necessarily fall? We rarely ask because we’ve never learned to see beyond ourselves, understanding that cost starts with understanding how we imagined our place in the world. Human beings have become a species capable of deciding the fate of almost everything around us: deciding where forests remain, where roads are built, where rivers flow, where wildlife may move, which animals are confined, and which habitats are altered for human purposes. Yet the power to decide does not necessarily create a right to decide. Beneath these choices lies an anthropocentric hierarchy where human interests are treated as primary while the interests of other living beings are considered secondary whenever they conflict with human preferences. Against this hierarchy, I rely on Martha C. Nussbaum’s capabilities approach to examine whether human interests should automatically prevail when their pursuit restricts the fundamental capabilities of animals. In Justice for Animals: Our Collective Responsibility , Martha places animals in the sphere of justice and argues that justice requires more than preventing suffering. It requires securing the conditions necessary for animals to flourish according to their species-specific nature. The precise content of flourishing necessarily differs between each species. A bird requires opportunity to fly, a fish requires an aquatic environment in which it can swim and behave according to its nature, and a wild animal requires habitat, movement, ecological relationships, and the ability to exist without constant human control. For Martha, the problem is not simply suffering. It is capability deprivation. The human domination over animals is not accidental; it is structural and deeply embodied in our political, cultural, social, and economic systems. It does not arise merely from individual cruelty but from institutional arrangements designed around human benefits. Around the world, animal laws and conservation policies are structured within an anthropocentric framework. Animals are protected, conserved, and regulated not as right-bearing beings, but as resources to be managed for human benefits. Like, in Pakistan, animals are largely protected through welfare-based laws, not through a capabilities-based framework. The primary legislation, such as the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1890 largely focuses on preventing visible cruelty rather than ensuring the flourishing of animals. Similarly, the provincial laws prioritize conservation of wildlife for human benefit rather than justice for animals themselves. The absence of a capabilities-based legal framework means that animals are still treated as objects of ownership and trade. Fish and birds sold on Pakistani streets are not perceived as beings whose rights are violated; instead, they are seen as commodities. They are viewed as property rather than beings of justice, where exploitation becomes habitual, invisible, and unquestioned. Human interests are not morally uniform. Human beings require food, shelter, health, security, transportation, livelihood, and infrastructure. But human societies also pursue convenience, entertainment, aesthetic preferences, commercial profits, and cultural habits. These interests cannot carry the same moral weight. A preference for cheap entertainment cannot automatically be placed on the same level as an animal’s basic freedom of movement. Fish trapped inside transparent plastic bags, under the complete control of a fish vendor on the streets of Lahore. Their aquatic life is reduced to a small plastic world where they remain alive, but are deprived of the space and freedom to live according to their nature. Photo by the author. Commercial tourism cannot automatically justify disturbing wildlife. Infrastructure development cannot justify destroying habitat where an alternative route or design is available. Martha’s framework, combined with necessity and proportionality principle, distinguishes the moral weight of different human claims. First, the human interest must be legitimate and sufficiently important. Secondly, the particular interference with animal capabilities must actually be necessary to achieve that interest. Lastly, where a less harmful and reasonable alternative exists, the more harmful practice should not be permitted merely because it is cheaper, easier, or customary. These tests distinguish human interests into non-essential, significant but non-vital, and vital human interests. Martha makes it clear that unnecessary human interests carry no moral or legal exception when they exploit an animal’s capabilities. Zoo confinement is a clear example of how entertainment and profit function as human interests that undermine animal rights. These animals are removed from their natural habitats and placed in artificial, restrictive environments, often in noisy and polluted urban settings. Zoos deny their freedom of movement, bodily integrity, and natural behavior’s, reducing them to spectacles for human amusement and revenue generation. The same analysis applies to the roadside sale of birds and fish. Birds confined in cages and fish sold in plastic bags are alive but incapable of flourishing. Even when sellers claim livelihood necessity, this interest remains non-essential because alternative businesses are available. The human right to business or livelihood cannot justify the exploitation of sentient beings. When business models depend on violating animal capabilities, they are illegal and should be prohibited. Justice requires banning such practices and supporting alternative livelihoods that do not rely on animal suffering. The commercial activities in protected wildlife areas reflect another form of human interest. Glamping and overcrowding disrupt wildlife migration patterns, feeding habits, breeding cycles, and freedom. While it generates profits, these benefits are not necessary for human survival and cannot justify the erosion of animal capabilities. Deforestation and unchecked urbanization also conflict with animals flourishing. They are built upon a hierarchy that privileges human expansion over interspecies justice. When forests and green belts are cleared for commercial use, animals lose the ecological foundation necessary for their existence. Habitat destruction fragments ecosystems, eliminates nesting and breeding grounds, and increases starvation and human-wildlife conflict. When forests are valued only for timber, and land and rivers are valued for commercial use, animals are reduced to externalities. In these cases, the principle is clear: human interest must be necessary and regulated. Economic gain, entertainment, and convenience cannot justify the deprivation of animal capabilities, particularly when alternatives exist or when such practices serve no essential human needs. If animal exploitation becomes normal and the state fails to regulate unnecessary human interests, the animal’s existence will become impossible. The limitation on human interests does not mean eliminating human freedom, but it means regulating and restricting activities that commodify living beings unnecessarily. Martha’s theory reminds us that animals are not objects of convenience; they are subjects whose capabilities impose limits on our ambition. The fish trapped in plastic, birds in cages, and zoo animals remind us that flourishing is a right, not a privilege, and human interest, no matter how convenient or profitable, must stop where the capabilities of other sentient beings begin. Limiting unnecessary and exploitative human interests is not a moral preference but a legal obligation in a just society committed to interspecies dignity and coexistence. It underscores that human freedom, while important, is not absolute and must yield when it conflicts with the flourishing of other species. The post When Humans Rise, Must Another Life Fall? Rethinking Human Interests and Animal Flourishing in an Anthropocentric World appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Sustainable Polymers and Natural Rubber Chart a Path Toward Greener Materials Reading Time: 3 minutes Sustainable polymers and natural rubber are moving to the center of materials science, as new research shows how to design them to reduce their environmental footprint. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber took center stage at a joint symposium between researchers in France and Thailand. The University of Haute-Alsace and Kasetsart University co-hosted the online event across May 2026. The program covered a wide range of materials topics, from energy materials to nanotechnology. One theme stood out clearly across the sessions. Scientists are now designing polymers not just for performance, but for durability, repairability, and better end-of-life outcomes. Dr. Wirasak Smitthipong of Kasetsart University presented one of the symposium’s central ideas. His team studies smart polymers that respond to light and can heal themselves when damaged. These self-healing materials include rubber and hydrogel systems. Special molecular bonds allow damaged sections to reconnect and recover their function, much like scar tissue mending itself. That self-repair ability matters beyond the lab. If a material can signal damage and fix itself, it may not need replacing as often. This applies especially to coatings, adhesives, and composite products, where small damage often forces the replacement of a much larger item. Light also played a starring role in another presentation. Dr. Jacques Lalevée from the Institut de Science des Matériaux de Mulhouse, part of the University of Haute-Alsace, discussed new light-activated processing methods for high-performance materials. His work uses light to trigger chemical reactions in coatings, inks, adhesives, and 3D-printed parts. This approach offers precise control, produces little or no volatile organic compound release, and reacts faster than older methods. That same light-based technique can work with bio-based resins made from natural oils. This points toward manufacturing that uses less energy and allows for localized repairs rather than full replacement. Other researchers tackled the opposite end of a material’s life. Dr. Amornrat Lertworasirikul of Kasetsart University studies how to make polylactic acid, a common bio-based plastic known as PLA, break down more easily after use. PLA already appears in packaging, farming tools, and medical devices. Her team found that adding a small amount, just 3% by weight, of a plant-derived compound helped the plastic become more flexible and degrade faster in water. This research raises an important question for sustainable polymers and natural rubber alike. Should a material last for decades, break down quickly, or simply become easier to repair and reuse? The answer depends entirely on the product. Packaging that gets used once benefits from fast degradation, while structural materials benefit more from durability and repair options. Natural rubber also showed plenty of untapped potential. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber face the same fundamental design question: should a material last for decades, break down quickly, or be easier to repair and reuse? The new research shows that a 3% plant-derived additive can make plastic more flexible and water-degradable, suggesting the answer depends entirely on what the material is made to do. Photo by Lucas van Oort on Unsplash. Dr. Sutee Boonchui presented transparent, flexible films made by blending natural rubber with quantum dots, tiny particles that glow under light. These fluorescent films could improve road safety equipment, making traffic signs and markers more visible. The natural rubber base keeps the material flexible enough for real-world outdoor use. Medical safety also got a rubber-based upgrade. Dr. Kiadtisak Saenboonruang described multilayer gloves made from sustainable polymers and natural rubber, designed to block X-ray radiation more effectively. By layering in a nanoscale bismuth oxide additive, the gloves blocked more radiation than standard single-layer versions. The outer layers of pure natural rubber kept the gloves flexible and comfortable to wear. Tire manufacturing also came under the sustainability lens. Dr. Hassarutai Yangthong showed how fly ash, a waste byproduct from burning coal, can replace some of the zinc oxide typically used in tire rubber production. Zinc oxide use raises environmental concerns when it washes into waterways. Lifecycle analysis found that substituting fly ash lowered several measures of environmental harm, including toxicity to freshwater and marine life. Taken together, these projects reveal a shared philosophy. True sustainability depends on a material’s entire lifecycle, not simply whether it originates from renewable sources. A bio-based plastic that requires enormous energy to produce offers little advantage over conventional options. Likewise, a material that degrades too quickly may not suit long-term applications like construction or safety equipment. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber research is now moving toward this more complete picture. Scientists are learning to weigh performance, repairability, and lifespan together rather than treating them as separate goals. The symposium’s researchers plan to keep exploring how far these smart materials can go. As industries search for greener alternatives to conventional plastics and rubber, this kind of integrated thinking may prove essential to getting the balance right. The post Sustainable Polymers and Natural Rubber Chart a Path Toward Greener Materials appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age Reading Time: 3 minutes From picture books for toddlers to a 400-page field guide, new bat conservation books invite readers of every age into the surprisingly wondrous world of the only flying mammal. Bat conservation books rarely dominate bestseller lists, but a fresh crop of titles released this year proves the subject deserves far more shelf space than it typically gets. Bat Conservation International recently rounded up a dozen standout titles spanning children’s picture books to dense scientific references, each aiming to replace fear of bats with fascination. For younger readers, several bat conservation books lean into storytelling and gentle life lessons. Stellaluna, considered among the first children’s books centered on bats, follows a baby fruit bat raised temporarily among birds after falling from her mother’s roost, ultimately learning that differences need not prevent friendship. I’m Not Scary follows a lonely bat who simply wants companionship despite living somewhere admittedly spooky, offering warm illustrations built around a familiar theme: kindness overcoming fear. Other bat conservation books for children tackle real conservation challenges directly. Bat Count: A Citizen Science Story introduces young readers to white-nose syndrome, the disease that has devastated North American bat populations, following a girl preparing for a community bat count who learns both the crisis facing bats and how ordinary people can help through citizen science. Amara and the Bats follows a similar arc, as a young bat enthusiast discovers her new neighborhood’s bat roosts have vanished due to tree removal, then finds inspiration in other young people already working to protect local bat populations. Additional titles for younger audiences round out the reading list. Little Red Bat explores the dilemma facing bat species that must choose between migration and hibernation as autumn arrives, weaving in facts about tree-roosting habits and camouflage along the way. The Bat Book, narrated from the perspective of a juvenile bat living under a bridge in Austin, Texas, directly addresses common misconceptions children repeat about bats being weird or scary. For adult readers and dedicated naturalists, bat conservation books shift toward deeper scientific territory. The Secret Lives of Bats follows renowned bat photographer and biologist Merlin Tuttle’s decades-long career, beginning with a teenage cave discovery outside Knoxville, Tennessee, that launched a lifetime devoted to bat ecology and conservation across encounters ranging from Kentucky moonshiners to charging elephants. The Weird and Wonderful World of Bats takes a curiosity-driven approach, devoting individual chapters to each bat sense, including echolocation, alongside candid explorations of bat mating behavior and social communication. For naturalists and dedicated readers, recent bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family and Bat Island document the diversity of nearly 1,500 known bat species through detailed photography, distribution maps, and firsthand field research. Photo courtesy of Bat Conservation International . The Genius Bat follows an ecologist’s research travels from Israeli deserts to tropical rainforests, examining how scientists design experiments to study bats’ extraordinary sensory and behavioral adaptations. For readers wanting comprehensive identification resources, bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family organize the roughly 1,500 known bat species by suborder, pairing close-up photography with distribution maps and details on diet, anatomy, and physiology. Bat Island narrows its focus dramatically, documenting the 76 bat species found on a single small island in Panama’s Lake Gatun through cinematic photography and firsthand research from Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute scientists. Rounding out the collection, Bats: An Illustrated Guide to All Species offers a 400-page reference dividing global bat diversity along modern phylogenetic lines, paired with extensive photography documenting species across every studied region. Together, these bat conservation books reflect a broader shift in how bats are represented in popular literature, moving decisively away from Halloween-season stereotypes toward genuine appreciation for animals that pollinate plants, disperse seeds, and consume enormous quantities of agricultural pests nightly. Whether introducing a child to their first bat-loving picture book character or offering seasoned naturalists a comprehensive species reference, this year’s releases make clear that meaningful conservation storytelling can also be genuinely engaging reading, proving that getting curious about bats might be the easiest first step toward protecting them. The post Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Αφού καεί το κερί, ο άνθρακας μένει πάνω του, και πρέπει να αφαιρέσετε αυτόν τον μαύρο άνθρακα από το φως, ώστε το φως να ανάψει ξανά." Το μάντρα του έμαθε να πειραματίζεται τόσο με την αφαίρεση του άνθρακα όσο και με το φωτισμό του jyoti -- το φως…
items.descriptionOriginal: Early on in school, Gaurav Marathe embraced a Viraja mantra translated by a teacher: "Humans are like a candle. After the candle burns, carbon stays on it, and you have to remove that black carbon from the light so the light again illuminates." The mantra taught him to experiment with both removing the carbon and illuminating the jyoti -- the light that exists within. In one of many experiments, he challenged students to remove the carbon of a task-driven, rule-driven festival on a campus where he taught. "Let's do that experiment. Let it be the kind of carnival where nobody is charging anything. No cost price, nothing. If anybody wants to pay, they pay. If they don't, they don't. Let's believe in that spirit." It was successful beyond anyone's imagination, and became a "Soul Carnival" where the focus is on giving over profiting. "Perhaps that's the point of these experiments — not to have all the answers, but to keep creating spaces where we can go close to inner jyoti a little more."

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article kicks off The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. It was winter break, and Dilan Mehta had time on his hands. His dad was packing for a mission trip to Kenya, where he’d been volunteering with Kenya Relief , a medical organization that runs a school in Migori, for years. Dilan packed a bag of stuffed animals for the children there. Then he glanced at his 3D printer. He started designing LEGO-inspired sets, printing each one out, and tucking them in alongside the stuffed animals. Somewhere between one print and the next, a different thought took shape. The school had students who could use a curriculum, and his dad had room in a suitcase. That’s how a 3D printer ended up in Migori, Kenya, and why it’s still being used to teach students today. What is Student Makers? Student Makers is a nonprofit that offers free STEM workshops to students across the United States, Kenya, and India, and every instructor is a former student. Most of them are still in high school. The organization was founded in California in 2019 by Anthony Neil Tan, then a high school senior. There was no space at his school where students interested in technology and making could come together to learn, so he built one. He called it the Maker Hub Club Initiative, secured a $5,000 grant from a social impact scholarship, and got it off the ground. The framework was three steps: learn a skill , make a project, showcase it. He was in his first year of college when he started handing it off. Serve: the fourth pillar Dilan didn’t find Student Makers; rather, Anthony found him. Roughly six years ago, Dilan was only in 8th grade and had entered an Autodesk design contest with a 3D-printed fingerboard, one that used flexible filament on the grip surface to behave like rubber. Anthony came across it and reached out. Would Dilan want to join a group where students build things and learn from each other? He joined, took the 3D printing course, came back as an instructor, and eventually rebuilt the entire curriculum from scratch around design thinking rather than output. A few years later, he was running the organization. But he felt that the project’s mission needed some rethinking. The original framework had three steps: learn, make, showcase. Dilan added a fourth, serve, because the workshops were primarily reaching students who already had resources, and that wasn’t what he’d signed up for. His dad’s Kenya-bound suitcase gave him the opening for a bigger idea to launch. Teaching through rain and static When Dilan sent that 3D printer to Kenya Relief Academy, he wasn’t thinking about it as a program. He was thinking about a school with 800 students, roughly 170 to 190 of them orphaned children, consistently ranked the top primary school in its region out of more than 800, and without any STEM infrastructure. His dad’s Kenya Relief contacts connected him to the teachers there, and he started meeting with them remotely three times a week. Every session ran over video call, Dilan in the US and the teachers in Migori, and when the Wi-Fi dropped, which it often would, they’d wait, reconnect, and keep going. He trained them in Autodesk Fusion 360, Tinkercad, and 3D printer operation, working through how to teach all of it to a classroom he’s never seen in person. “They constantly have Wi-Fi issues,” Dilan said. “Anytime there’s rain, they basically lose connection. Just being patient, being empathetic , understanding that that’s just the situation.” Ruth Agongo, a teacher at Kenya Relief Academy, described what it looked like from the other end. “You are a game-changer,” she said. “Whatever you have taught us, we are putting into action because the kids are really excited by the technology.” Jacob A few semesters into his time at Georgia Tech, once Dilan had actually taken a step back from Student Makers and was serving mostly as an advisory board member, Dilan got a message from the teachers at Kenya Relief Academy. They needed help with a science fair project: an Arduino-based robot that could navigate a garden, measure soil moisture at different points, and decide where to water. Dilan didn’t know much about robotics, but he was at Georgia Tech, so he asked around. Twelve students from the university ended up on the project. They built components in Atlanta while the Kenya team built in Migori, troubleshot over video call, and sent physical supplies through a similar suitcase network that had carried the original printer. That team placed third at regionals of the Kenya Science and Engineering Fair. One of the students on it, a ninth-grader named Jacob, now leads Kenya Relief Academy’s robotics team. His dream is to become a rocket engineer at NASA. A family connection in India Rohan Naegle, who led Student Makers before the current team took over, brought a similar program to Dr. R.V. Shah English Medium School in rural Gujarat, India, after his grandfather put him in touch with the school. Live 3D printing classes run there over video call, using the same structure. More than 25 secondary students have completed the program, and a donated printer stays at the school. Both the Kenya and India connections came organically, through family. How the pipeline runs Aarush Goel, who now leads the high school chapters, came in the same way Dilan did: a friend pulled him in to co-teach a Python workshop, and he showed up not entirely sure what he was doing. “You just start teaching and everything goes into place,” he said. He’s since led five workshop tracks across the US, and next year he’ll start a Student Makers chapter at his own college. Instructors are recruited the same way at every level. At the end of each cycle, a call goes out for anyone who wants to come back and teach the next round. Usually one or two students say yes. They already know the program from the inside, which tends to make them good at the part that matters most: building something new students actually want to stay in. Anthony, watching from his current advisory role, put it plainly. “It’s more relatable, a high schooler showing a middle schooler how to do some 3D printing than someone who’s already a young adult,” he said. “So it’s nice keeping that peer-to-peer instruction model.” He’s 25. The organization he started as a high school senior just turned seven. Growing the network Student Makers recently joined a partnership with Youth Technology Corps Global Alliance , a network of schools across roughly 12 countries that has been running a similar peer-learning model since 1998. YTC has been doing this for nearly three decades and has school connections worldwide; Student Makers brings the volunteers and the curriculum. This fall, programs are launching under the partnership in Mexico, Colombia, Ethiopia, and Illinois, with the 3D printing and CAD curriculum going into Mexico specifically. “I would have never imagined that we would have this extensive of a reach,” Anthony said. The reach he couldn’t have imagined started with a simple observation: students interested in technology and making didn’t have a space to come together. So he built one. Why Student Makers opens this year’s series Each year, The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers series runs in the weeks before Thanksgiving, and this year, for the first time, every person in it is 30 or under. When Aarush reached out to us with the Student Makers story last summer, we spent weeks talking with the people who built this organization and were honestly floored by their dedication, hard work, and willingness to serve others. The five other changemakers in this year’s series were nominated by The Optimist Daily community, but Student Makers was not. It was the story that inspired the decision behind this year’s “30 and under” theme. This article skims the surface of the deeper story behind Student Makers. If you want to learn more about their incredible work, hang tight for a podcast episode featuring the voices behind this initiative. It’ll be coming out in early 2027. In the meantime, you can learn more and support their work at www.studentmakers.org . items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Αυτό το άρθρο είναι μέρος της σειράς Local Changemakers 2026 του The Optimist Daily, δίνοντας έμφαση στους δημιουργούς αλλαγής 30 ετών και κάτω.
